title.en: Sefer Shemos, the book of geulah, in the days of Teves

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that Bereishis holds the roots and signs of what follows and that Shemos is the book of geulah. He explains that it is read in the dark, dangerous weeks of Teves, citing Sefer Chassidim and the Bnei Yissaschar, so that learning it lifts a Jew above the darkness, and notes that the Shechinah went down with Yaakov into exile.

title.en: Believing the geulah is already prepared

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the names of the shevatim hint at geulah, and explains that in exile a Jew must believe that while Jews groan under their labor, the geulah is already being prepared in Heaven, as at the burning bush. With the Ba'al Shem Tov's rule that a person is where his thoughts are, he says that keeping one's mind in Sefer Shemos lifts him out of the darkness.

title.en: The tzaddikim are gone, but Hashem lives

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the parsha is a living Torah for today: the questions asked then about Jewish suffering are asked today about other lands. On 'Vayamos Yosef' he describes the loss of the generation of great tzaddikim, and brings the Midrash that the G-d of Israel did not die; Hashem still leads His people, and their Torah and avodah light the way.

title.en: Amram's drashos and the scoffers in Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Amram and Aharon gave drashos to strengthen the Jews in Egypt, while assimilated, well-placed Jews and writers urged them to join Egyptian culture and mocked the old faith, crying out over the decrees. He asks what Amram could answer, and suggests he said what the Chasam Sofer writes on 'bikesh Yaakov leishev beshalvah' with the Ramban's rule.

title.en: Bereishis as a picture of the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through Bereishis as a preview of Jewish history: Avraham's descent to Egypt, the bris bein habesarim, Yitzchak's love for Esav as the second Beis Hamikdash, Yaakov with Lavan as the long exile, the war with Esav and Dinah as the wars before Moshiach. When Yaakov expected peace, Yosef's troubles began, because this world cannot hold the joy of the days of Moshiach; Amram taught this to the Jews in Egypt.

title.en: The Egypt generation repairs earlier sins

summary.en: The 'enlightened' Jews were not comforted, but to those who remained Amram revealed that the generation in Egypt carried the souls of the dor haflagah and the generation of the Flood, so the bricks and mortar and the babies thrown into the river completed their tikun. The Mashgiach adds what the Chasam Sofer brings, that the victims of the decrees of 5408-5409 were souls from the time of the Churban.

title.en: A name holds a person's mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that Rus was named for Dovid who would come from her, learned from 'asher sam shamos ba'aretz'. He explains that every person is sent with a mission rooted in his name, that names change with one's mission as the angel told Yaakov, and that the Jews in Egypt kept their names; calling a Jew by his Jewish name draws down its influence.

title.en: Pharaoh's names for the midwives

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains, as the Chasam Sofer and the Bnei Yissaschar both say, why the Torah tells that Pharaoh named the midwives Shifrah and Puah before ordering them to kill: he gave them Egyptian names to draw them under the power of evil. He then turns to today's 'progressive' questioners who cite the Holocaust to deny the Torah's authority and the old leaders.

title.en: Shamos: wonders that are missions

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew and every generation has a mission, some to suffer to prepare a later salvation. From Tehillim 46 he distinguishes churban, a destruction one understands, from shamah, a destruction that arouses wonder, related to shamayim; reading 'al tikri shamos ela shemos', he explains that the bewildering destructions are missions whose answers will come in the time of tikun.

title.en: Yosef in Egypt, and Dasan and Aviram

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that 'veYosef haya veMitzrayim' teaches Yosef's righteousness, and asks why it belongs in the book of geulah, which speaks of the nation. He then raises a second question: Rashi identifies the two quarreling men as Dasan and Aviram by their leaving over the manna, though they did far worse things later.

title.en: Bitachon, the key in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls bitachon the key word of exile, from 'bitchu vaHashem adei ad' and Dovid's trust since birth. He explains the midwives' answer that the Hebrew women are like animals, and says that in the days of Teves, when serving Hashem is hard, one needs bitachon and chizuk in avodas Hashem, bringing the Midrash that even a rasha who trusts in Hashem is surrounded by kindness.

title.en: The Apter Rav and Hashem's partner

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a simple Jew who sold brandy and whose blessings were fulfilled; the Apter Rav visited him and learned that he had taken Ribono shel Olam as his partner, giving Hashem's half of every sale to tzedakah. He then brings the Chovos Halevavos that the One who cared for a person in his helpless childhood will not abandon him now.

title.en: Goshen Jews and those who broke out

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the believing Jews in Goshen who kept the tradition Yaakov taught them, bringing the Chiddushei HaRim that Yosef presented his weakest brothers to Pharaoh so they would stay apart. Others, like Dasan and Aviram, studied and climbed to wealth among the Egyptians; he brings the Gemara that being lowly in exile is a blessing, the lessons of Spain and Germany, and the leaders' fight against studying among the Egyptians.

title.en: The root of Dasan and Aviram: no bitachon

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers why Rashi identifies Dasan and Aviram by the manna: leaving it over shows the root of their fall, a lack of bitachon that made them worry about tomorrow, seek careers and go where chutzpah is taught. He adds that chutzpah precedes geulah, and that they claimed Yosef as their precedent for staying a Jew in high places.

title.en: Forced, like Yosef, or by choice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that exile among the nations is harmful, but Jews were sent there by Hashem with a mission, and one who is sent has special protection, as Yosef was. He brings what he heard from a grandson of the Chofetz Chaim, that forced secular study does not harm, and concludes that the Torah mentions Yosef to distinguish the forced from Dasan and Aviram, who chose.

title.en: The Jew who would not work on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew in America decades earlier who could not find a job without working on Shabbos and resolved that as long as there was bread in a garbage can he would not desecrate Shabbos. He concludes that a Jew who is not forced may not endanger his soul, and that even in Mitzrayim every Jew has a mission and should bind himself to the geulah.

catalogTitle: The Depth of the כיבוד אב of יוסף and our Connection to the אבות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef asked for his own bones to be carried to Eretz Yisrael as a hiddur in honoring his father, since a son's bones are an extension of his father, and from there that Yaakov Avinu never died because every Jew carries a part of him.

abstract.en: On Shabbos Chazak of Vayechi the Mashgiach asks a series of questions on Yosef's answer to Yaakov. Instead of simply promising to bury his father in Eretz Yisrael, Yosef seems to speak of himself, then makes his brothers rather than his sons swear to carry his bones, imposes this on them as well, and speaks of his 'bones' although a tzaddik's body does not decay, as the Mashgiach illustrates with accounts of tzaddikim found intact. He answers with the Gemara that a person's bones come from his father: Yosef's bones are Yaakov's extension, so carrying them completes Yaakov's burial, a task for Yaakov's sons. He then brings the Gemara that Yaakov Avinu did not die: in the drush of Torah he lives in every Jewish heart. This ties to Melave Malka, where Yaakov's past and David HaMelech's future meet, and to teshuvah: since Yaakov lives on, no Jew is ever too late.

en: According to the Gemara a person's bones come from his father, so a son's bones are an extension of the father's body.
Yosef's request that his own bones be carried to Eretz Yisrael was not about himself but a hiddur in his father's burial, completing it.

Yosef gave the task to his brothers because burying a father is the sons' obligation more than the grandsons', and all the brothers had to be carried up so that nothing of Yaakov would remain in Mitzrayim.
Yaakov Avinu did not die: besides the trace of life left in his body, he left a part of himself in every living Jew.
At Melave Malka the Jews take Yaakov, their past, into the weekdays, and draw hope from David HaMelech, their future, both of whom never died.
Because Yaakov lives on in every Jew, no Jew can say it is too late for him to return to Hashem.

title.en: Shabbos Chazak and Yaakov's last request

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the strength to be drawn from Shabbos Chazak and from Yaakov Avinu. He then reads Yaakov's request not to be buried in Mitzrayim, and Yosef's reply 'I will do as you say', which the Daas Zekeinim reads as Yosef promising that he too will be carried to Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Questions on Yosef's reply and his bones

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yosef, at his father's last will, seems to turn to himself; why he made his brothers rather than his sons swear to carry his bones, imposing on them what is only a chumrah; and why he was punished with being called 'bones' in his lifetime and what insult there is in speaking of one's own bones.

title.en: A tzaddik's body does not decay

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Bava Metzia and accounts of tzaddikim, the Rebbe Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk and others, whose bodies were found intact, and the grain Yosef stored that did not rot, and a Stoliner signature that stayed black. He concludes with the question: Yosef knew his whole body would remain, so why did he speak only of his bones?

title.en: Bones from the father: Yosef's hiddur

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers all the questions with the Gemara that a person's bones come from his father. Yosef's bones are Yaakov's extension, so by having them carried to Eretz Yisrael Yosef was not thinking of himself but adding a hiddur to his father's burial, and he said 'my bones' to make clear he meant the mitzvah.

title.en: Why the brothers, and all of them

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a father's burial is the sons' obligation more than the grandsons', so Yosef gave the completion of Yaakov's burial to Yaakov's sons, his brothers. Since all the brothers' bones also belong to Yaakov, Rashi's 'with you' shows they too were carried up, so that nothing of Yaakov would remain in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Yaakov Avinu did not die

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the trace of life, kusta d'chayusa, that remains in a body after death, which is why one davens at a tzaddik's kever, and tells of the Yismach Moshe at the kever of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech. He then brings the Gemara that Yaakov Avinu did not die, and explains that beyond his kever Yaakov left a trace of himself in every living Jew.

title.en: Pshat, drush and the Avos in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Torah has pshat and drush, the Torah she'b'al peh that comes from the Jewish heart; in pshat Yaakov was buried, in drush he lives in every Jewish heart. Avraham gave love, Yitzchak fear, and Yaakov the Jewish neshama itself, so every child of Yaakov is a Jew, and while Jewish children live, Yaakov lives.

title.en: Melave Malka: Yaakov the past, David the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at Melave Malka, the meal for the luz bone, Jews sing 'Al tira avdi Yaakov' and speak of those who never died. Yaakov is the past from which Jews draw and David HaMelech the future they are heading toward; this is why the parsha of Yaakov's passing is called Vayechi.

title.en: Shabbos does not die either

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a proof from the Melave Malka meal, held after Shabbos for Shabbos: just as Yaakov did not die, Shabbos does not go away. Every Jew should be proud that Yaakov is in him as a father, and he explains why the seforim say Melave Malka reaches higher than the other meals of Shabbos.

title.en: Into the week and golus with Yaakov; never too late

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Jews carry Yaakov's fresh brachos into the weekdays and into the golus of Shemos without fear. Since a Jew never dies, no Jew can say it is too late; the weeks of teshuvah that begin after Chazak are a time to return to the source of the neshama.

catalogTitle: בשם של אדם נרמז שליחתו ונתינת כח לעשותו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person's name hints at his mission in the world and gives him the strength to carry it out, and applies this to the names in Sefer Shemos and to the bewildering suffering of whole generations.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that every person has a mission hinted in his name, drawing on Rashi that an angel's name changes with its mission, and on the power of ruach hakodesh in naming a child, illustrated by stories of the Chiddushei HaRim and the Tiferes Shlomo. Through the Agra deKallah and the Chasam Sofer he explains why Pharaoh spoke twice to the midwives: first to give them Egyptian names, so that he could then order them to kill. From the Gemara's reading of shamos as shemos he teaches that generations of bewildering destruction, including the Mashgiach's own, also carry a name and a mission. He explains why Sefer Shemos repeats the names of the tribes, how one name can carry different combinations, and that a believing Jew is never truly lost, as a story of a tzaddik on the wrong train shows. He closes with how a person can recognize his own mission.

en: Every person has a mission in the world, and it is hinted in his name, which acts like a battery giving him strength to fulfill it.
Pharaoh first gave the Jewish midwives Egyptian names to draw impurity onto them, and only then ordered them to kill; because they kept their Jewish names, they did not obey.
The Gemara reads 'shamos' (desolations) as 'shemos' (names): generations of bewildering destruction also have a name and a mission.
The names at the start of Sefer Shemos are names of redemption, unlike the same names in Vayigash, and the same name can carry a different combination and so a different calling.
A Jew who lives with emunah and hashgacha pratis knows that wherever he goes he is on Hashem's mission and is never truly lost.
A person can recognize his mission by the strong desire he has for a certain avodah and by the obstacles that keep blocking it.

candidateTopics: a person's mission in the world
suffering of generations and the Holocaust
permutations of Hashem's Name and the months

title.en: A person's mission is hinted in his name

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens that every person's mission is hinted in his name, bringing Rashi that an angel's name changes with each mission, and that parents naming a child have ruach hakodesh. He tells of the Chiddushei HaRim's advice on naming, explains why a sick person is given an added name, and tells how the Tiferes Shlomo knew a sick man's name from the 'Sefer Shemos'.

title.en: Why Pharaoh spoke twice to the midwives

summary.en: Bringing the Agra deKallah and the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains the double 'vayomer' in the passuk: a person may have a name of kedushah and a name of tumah, so Pharaoh first gave the midwives Egyptian names and only then ordered them to kill the Jewish boys. They kept their Jewish names and therefore did not obey.

title.en: Shamos: destruction that bewilders

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that a name has an effect, from 'asher sam shamos ba'aretz' read as 'shemos', and explains that 'shamos' means a destruction people are astonished at. He lists such generations: Mitzrayim, the Crusades, the Inquisition, the decrees of 1648-49, and his own generation's unprecedented churban, and says that despite the wonder there is a Ribono shel Olam who runs the world.

title.en: Each generation has a name and a mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings known answers for earlier generations: the Zohar that the generation of Mitzrayim were gilgulim of the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion, that the generation of the churban were those of the Golden Calf, and that the decrees of 1648-49 struck the souls of the biryonim. Hashem runs the world with a reckoning, and every generation, like every person, has a name and a mission; in his generation's case, a gathering of souls sent to wipe out a flaw in creation.

title.en: Names of redemption and combinations of a name

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Sefer Shemos repeats the names already listed in Vayigash, and answers with the Ramban that Shemos is the book of redemption and with the Midrash that ties each tribe's name to the geulah. Two people with the same name can have different missions, as the twelve combinations of Hashem's four-letter Name show, with Nisan a month of chesed and Teves a month of din.

title.en: Shem means 'there': the tzaddik on the wrong train

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'shem' is related to 'sham', far away, like 'shamayim', so a name and its mission are beyond our grasp, yet a Jew must know that everything is hashgacha pratis and that wherever he goes he is on a mission. He tells of a great tzaddik who took a three-day train in the wrong direction in Russia and stayed calm, saying he must have something to do there.

title.en: Hagar's wandering: a believer never strays

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the same tzaddik's explanation of 'vatelech vateta' about Hagar: why do Chazal say she returned to her father's idolatry, when the plain meaning that she got lost is fine? Because a Jew who believes in Hashem never truly gets lost; one's feet always carry him where Hashem wants, so straying can only mean turning away from Hashem.

title.en: How to recognize one's own mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from sefarim hakedoshim that a person recognizes his mission where he has a strong desire yet keeps meeting obstacles, since the Satan works hardest there, and that each person's desire follows the root of his soul. He closes that the answer to why Jews suffered in Mitzrayim and throughout history is 'shemos', a mission from Hashem, and that when Moshiach comes the answers will be known.

catalogTitle: שיטת פרעה "אני עשיתיני" - Evolution

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Pharaoh's claim 'I made myself' as the evolutionism of his day, a refusal to acknowledge a Creator that no logic could break, only the makos, and applies it to the Pharaoh within every person and to the hester panim of our generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the theme of Vaera: Hashem reveals Himself. The Avos saw Him even within hester panim, but Moshe protested the concealment out of mesiras nefesh for Klal Yisrael, and was told he would not enter Eretz Yisrael, which in turn saved the generation of the desert; this links to Avraham giving water through a messenger and to the unfulfilled fifth expression of redemption. He then turns to Pharaoh, a great sage who said of himself 'I made myself' (Yechezkel), and explains him as the evolutionist of his time, who denied a first cause because he did not want obligations. Logic could not move him, only makos, because a klipah clouds emunah. The Midrash on 'kaved lev Pharaoh', the Satmar Rav's explanation, and examples of design in nature follow. He concludes that every person has a Pharaoh to strike during Shovavim through effort in avodah, and that our generation, living in great hester panim, must believe without seeing.

en: The Avos found Hashem within every state of concealment, while Moshe protested the hester panim out of mesiras nefesh for Klal Yisrael.
Pharaoh's claim 'I made myself' was not madness but the position of an evolutionist: denying a first cause and claiming that the world, and he himself, came about on their own.
The denial comes from not wanting to accept obligation, not from logic, so it cannot be answered with logic but only with makos.
A klipah born of ervas ha'aretz clouds a person's emunah, so neither suffering nor statistics helped the Egyptians until all ten makos had passed.
Every person has a Pharaoh within him, and the weeks of Shovavim are the time to strike it, today through effort in tefillah, Torah, chesed and breaking one's desires, and through mitzvos.
The generation of the desert did not believe though it saw miracles; our generation lives in great hester panim and its task is to believe without seeing.

candidateTopics: evolution and denial of a Creator
Moshe's mesiras nefesh for Klal Yisrael

title.en: Vaera: Hashem reveals Himself

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the parsha answers Moshe's complaint about hester panim: the Avos saw Hashem even in concealment, through nature. Moshe protested out of mesiras nefesh for Klal Yisrael, and Rashi says he was told he would not lead the war against the thirty-one kings.

title.en: Water through a messenger, and the fifth cup

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham, the great man of chesed, gave water to his guests through a messenger, and answers that he hated their avodah zarah and did not want to show it. Measure for measure, water in the desert came through Moshe, and his not entering Eretz Yisrael saved the generation; the fifth expression of redemption, 'veheveisi', remains for the time of Eliyahu.

title.en: Pharaoh says: I made myself

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the revelation of Vaera is directed at Pharaoh, whose name means uncovering. He brings the haftarah in Yechezkel where Pharaoh says 'my river is mine and I made myself', and asks how a great sage, king of the center of civilization, could say such a thing; Rashi says he deified himself at the Nile.

title.en: Pharaoh, the evolutionist of his time

summary.en: Since history repeats itself, the Mashgiach explains Pharaoh as the evolutionist of his day: he denied a first cause for the same reason as today's evolutionists, because admitting a Creator obliges one to accept the Torah. Every falsehood needs a point of truth, and the Torah itself describes the world developing from water to plants, fish and man.

title.en: Not logic, only makos

summary.en: Pharaoh's whole system rested on the Nile as the beginning of everything, which even a child sees is madness. The Mashgiach explains that such people do not want to hear the truth so as not to keep mitzvos, so one cannot explain it to them with logic, only with makos; he compares Korach's followers, who sinned 'against their own souls'.

title.en: The klipah of ervas ha'aretz

summary.en: The purpose of every makah was that Pharaoh should acknowledge 'that I am Hashem in the midst of the land', yet he saw and suffered and still did not believe. The Mashgiach explains that a klipah held him back: Egypt was ervas ha'aretz, a place of pgam habris, which clouds emunah so that no logic helps.

title.en: The barad and the fifty-fifty chance

summary.en: Before the barad Moshe gave the Egyptians practical advice to bring their animals inside, yet some left them in the field. The Mashgiach asks how, after six makos all foretold exactly, anyone could ignore this, and compares drinking from one of two bottles when one is poison; the answer is the klipah, which would not lift until the full process of ten makos.

title.en: Kaved lev Pharaoh: a heart that is not a heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that reads 'kaved lev Pharaoh' as 'Pharaoh's heart is a liver', with its parable of the lion, the donkey at the toll bridge and the fox who ate its heart. He explains it with what he heard in the name of the Satmar Rav: every heart fears Hashem, and a heart without fear of Hashem is not a heart at all.

title.en: The deaf moth and the wonders of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites a sefer of one of the gedolei Yisrael about a night-flying moth that is deaf to everything except the sound of the bat that hunts it, and whose wings bear the image of a bird's eye. He adds the heart beating harder when running, fever, the body's repair system and involuntary muscles, all in harmony, and asks how people who say all this happened by chance would not take the chance with their animals; the answer is again the klipah.

title.en: The Pharaoh within, and Shovavim

summary.en: The Torah tells this for all generations because every person has a Pharaoh within him. The Mashgiach explains that the six weeks of Shovavim, from Shemos to Mishpatim, are the time to repair the pgam of ervas ha'aretz before Terumah, when a Mishkan can be built in the heart; once this was done with fasts, and today the makos are effort in tefillah, Torah, chesed and breaking one's desires.

title.en: Mitzvos, 'veheveisi' and the generation of the desert

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the true way to emunah is through mitzvos, as the Jews in Egypt were given Pesach and milah. He asks how the promise 'veheveisi' was made to a generation that never entered the land, and answers that those souls return in the generation of Moshiach. With Dovid Hamelech's words he explains that the generation of the desert lacked emunah despite seeing miracles, because emunah comes from a clean heart, not from seeing wonders.

title.en: Our generation: believing without seeing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that our generation is the reverse of the desert generation: it lives in the greatest hester panim, after millions of Jews were killed, and its task is to believe without seeing. Those who complain why the Jews let themselves be led away do so not out of mesiras nefesh but because they do not want the truth, which is written in Ha'azinu: 'how could one pursue a thousand' unless Hashem had handed them over.

title.en: The first exile as a sign for ours

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbeinu Bachya at the end of Parshas Shemos, that the exile of Egypt hints at our exile: we wait 'shomrim laboker' for a morning that passes, and the end of the exile is harder than all of it. He points to growing hatred of Jews and to 'good friends' among the nations who turned out otherwise, concluding that one can rely only on Hashem.

catalogTitle: המכות - נגוף למצרים ורפוא לישראל. (דרוש נפלא על ענין ירמיהו ונביאתו בחצר המטרה) [מס' ב”ב כ”ח]

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the makkos were a blow to Egypt and a healing for Israel, and builds a long derush on why Yirmiyahu received his greatest prophecies of consolation while imprisoned in the chatzar hamatarah, ending with Rashi's last words on chezkas habatim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Sefer Shemos as the book of redemption: whoever learns a parsha lives in its time, as Rebbi showed when he cursed Nevuchadnetzar only while reading Yirmiyahu. The makkos were a blow to Egypt and a healing for Israel, so learning them breaks the evil in a person. He brings the Chasam Sofer's question how one may mention the makkos, which are mazikim, and why Tehillim reorders them, and answers that for Jews they are pure healing; Tehillim reorders them only where they rebuke Israel or address the nations. Turning to Bava Basra 28, he asks why Rashi notes that Yirmiyahu's prophecy of the field came in the chatzar hamatarah. That was the room where Shlomo HaMelech planned the Beis HaMikdash; Tzidkiyahu placed Yirmiyahu there hoping for a prophecy of consolation, and indeed he received the greatest consolations, though not the annulment of the decree. Rashi, the soul of Shlomo and Yirmiyahu, ends his commentary with Hashem's chazakah on Eretz Yisrael.

en: Learning a parsha means living in its time: Sefer Shemos is the book of redemption, so learning it places a person in geulah.
Every makkah was a blow to Egypt and a healing for Israel, so learning the makkos is a power that breaks the evil within a person.
For Jews the makkos are not mazikim, so they may be told at any time; Tehillim changes their order only where Jews are rebuked or the nations are addressed.
The chatzar hamatarah was where Shlomo HaMelech planned the Beis HaMikdash, and Tzidkiyahu placed Yirmiyahu there so that in its merit he would receive a prophecy of consolation.
The chiddush of the field is that in the very hour of the siege Hashem was already preparing the redemption, a sign of His love and of His protest that the land remains His.
Rashi, whose soul was that of Shlomo HaMelech and Yirmiyahu, ends his commentary with chezkas habatim: Hashem never forgoes His chazakah, and everything taken from the Jews will return.

title.en: Sefer Shemos: living in the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Sefer Shemos is the book of redemption and that whoever learns Torah lives in the time he learns about. He proves it from Rebbi, who cursed Nevuchadnetzar only while reading Yirmiyahu, and says that this Shabbos one lives through the makkos of Pharaoh.

title.en: A blow to Egypt, a healing for Israel

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the ten makkos to the ten maamaros and the ten dibros and brings the pasuk that the makkos were a blow to Egypt and a healing for Israel. Learning them, he says, breaks the evil in a person, like the extra time added to Shabbos that removes the part of the goy within.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: may one mention the makkos?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's question: the makkos are mazikim, so how may they be mentioned outside the Seder, and why does Tehillim list them out of order? He tells how the Chasam Sofer rejected a student who stepped on sechach, and says he will try to answer without contradicting him.

title.en: Healing before the blow; the four cups

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Megillah that for Jews Hashem sends the healing before the blow, and the pasuk that the diseases of Egypt will not come upon Israel. He shows the same at the Seder: the cup from which drops are spilled for the makkos is the cup over which Hallel is said.

title.en: Why Tehillim changes the order

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the question on Tehillim: chapter 78 rebukes Israel for forgetting Hashem's wonders, which could arouse a kitrug, and chapter 105 speaks to the nations, for whom the makkos remain mazikim. When Jews tell the makkos, as in this parsha, they draw down salvation.

title.en: Living the parsha; Hashem's protest

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls on his listeners to live with the parsha: Pharaoh's hardened heart becomes for Jews a softened heart, and Va'eira also means 'I will appear', since the makkos will return before Moshiach. 'My firstborn son Israel' is Hashem's protest in galus that the nations hold no chazakah over the Jews, and what is learned below, such as chezkas habatim, is learned above.

title.en: Why Rashi mentions the chatzar hamatarah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Bava Basra that the three-year chazakah is learned from Yirmiyahu's purchase of the field, and asks why Rashi adds that the prophecy came in the chatzar hamatarah. He adds more questions: why Tzidkiyahu, a tzaddik, locked him up, why a prison was in the king's house, and why the Arizal pointed out this place in Yerushalayim.

title.en: The prophet of calamity and the field

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Yeshayahu, the prophet of consolation, with Yirmiyahu, the prophet of calamity, and says that in the chatzar hamatarah the picture turned. He reads the account of Chanamel's field and Yirmiyahu's prayer, and Hashem's reply that the city had stirred His anger from the day it was built, the day Shlomo married Pharaoh's daughter.

title.en: Consolations greater than Yeshayahu's

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the prophecies Yirmiyahu received there: the ingathering, one heart, an everlasting covenant, the voice of joy and of chosson and kallah, and Yerushalayim called 'Hashem Tzidkeinu'. He calls them consolations Yeshayahu himself did not say, and asks why they came specifically there.

title.en: What is new in the field? Two introductions

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the sign of the field adds, when every child knows from the Chumash that the Jews will return. He lays two foundations: a person's last words hold the essence of his life, as with Rabbah bar Nachmani and the Sfas Emes, and each prophecy comes according to the prophet's root, as Yoshiyahu sent to Chuldah rather than Yirmiyahu.

title.en: Yirmiyahu was Shlomo HaMelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the Arizal that Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, who had to see the destruction of the house he built. Shlomo was born under the best star and reached all he desired, which no other person ever did; his day is Shemini Atzeres, while Yirmiyahu's is Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Tzidkiyahu's plan

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the chatzar hamatarah as a cool hall in Shlomo's palace where Shlomo planned the Beis HaMikdash. Tzidkiyahu, a tzaddik, put Yirmiyahu there so that in Shlomo's merit he would receive a good prophecy, which unlike a bad one cannot be retracted, as in the dispute with Chananiah; he compares it to the Yismach Moshe sensing the holiness of a place where Reb Elimelech had davened.

title.en: Redemption prepared in the hour of destruction

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Tzidkiyahu was right: Yirmiyahu received unprecedented consolations. The chiddush is that while the siege and hunger were already on Yerushalayim, Hashem was preparing the redemption, a lasting protest that the Jews will return, guaranteed because the Shechinah is with them in galus; and 'matarah' is a name of the Shechinah who guards and waits.

title.en: Why the decree was not annulled

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tzidkiyahu erred in hoping to annul the decree. Yirmiyahu, sensing a time of favor, prayed to cancel it entirely, but Hashem answered that this very place, where Shlomo planned the house on the day His anger began, is itself the accuser, and like the Kohen Gadol's gold garments an accuser cannot become a defender.

title.en: Rashi, the soul of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Rashi was the soul of Shlomo HaMelech, hinted in the word Bereishis, and explains why Rashi became the teacher of all Israel, from the child learning Chumash to the scholar of Bava Basra. Rashi remembered being Shlomo and Yirmiyahu, and his last words on the Torah held the essence of his soul.

title.en: Rashi's last words: Hashem's chazakah

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Rashi's commentary ends in chezkas habatim, on Yirmiyahu in the chatzar hamatarah, because Hashem never forgoes His chazakah: the Jews and everything taken from them will return. Rashi's first Torah, on Bereishis, answers the nations' charge of theft, and his last teaches that the land and the Beis HaMikdash belong to the Jews.

catalogTitle: ויחי יעקב - The Eternity of צדיקים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef asked for his bones, the part of him that came from his father, to be carried out of Mitzrayim in honor of Yaakov, since a son is the continuation of his father and every Jew still carries something of Yaakov Avinu.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yaakov's request not to be buried in Mitzrayim and asks why Yosef answered by saying he too would be carried out, why he made his brothers rather than his sons swear, why he cared about his brothers' bones, and why he said 'my bones' rather than 'me'. He shows from Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon and from stories he witnessed about the Stoliner Rebbe and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech that a tzaddik's body does not decompose, so Yosef did not mean his bones alone. From the Gemara that the bones come from the father, and that a son is the continuation of his father, he answers all the questions: Yosef wanted no part of Yaakov to remain in impure Mitzrayim. Every Jew carries a residue of Yaakov, which can hold a person back in a test. He adds that Torah is alive, so this Shabbos we stand at the bedside of Yaakov and Yosef, and ends with a long explanation of the night of Nittel.

en: A tzaddik's body does not decompose; time leaves no mark on him, and so certainly Yosef remained intact.
According to the Gemara the bones come from the father, and since a son is the continuation of his father, that continuation lies in the bones.
Yosef asked that his bones be brought up so that no extension of Yaakov would remain in the impure land of Mitzrayim, in honor of his father and not for himself.
Yosef commanded his brothers rather than his sons because the mitzvah of honoring Yaakov rests more on his sons than on his grandsons, and he had all twelve brothers carried up.
Every Jew still carries a residue of Yaakov Avinu, and for that reason no Jew will remain on impure earth when Moshiach comes.
Torah is alive: learning it is not history but reliving the events, so this Shabbos one stands at the bedside of Yaakov and Yosef.

candidateTopics: son as the continuation of his father

title.en: Yaakov's request and Yosef's strange reply

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Yaakov's request not to be buried in Mitzrayim and the Midrash that Yosef answered by saying he too would have his bones carried up. He asks why Yosef gave no assurance, and why he made his brothers rather than his own children swear to it.

title.en: Why 'my bones', and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds two questions: why Yosef had his brothers' bones brought up as well, as Rashi learns from 'with you', and why he said 'my bones' rather than 'carry me' as Yaakov did. He brings the Gemara that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's body stayed intact for over twenty years before burial.

title.en: The Stoliner Rebbe found intact

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells what he saw when the Stoliner Rebbe, who had died of diabetes, was disinterred after sixteen months to be brought to Eretz Yisrael: his body was intact, his shrouds white, and the casket would not fit into the El Al plane.

title.en: The Rebbe Reb Elimelech and the Nazis

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew from Lizhensk, later supported by the Skverer Rebbe, who was forced by the Nazis to open the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's grave; after some 150 years the body lay intact and the Nazis fled. He concludes that time leaves no mark on a tzaddik.

title.en: Whatever Yosef touched endured

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the grain Yosef stored did not rot, and shows a letter whose signature by the Rebbe stayed black while the gabbai's writing browned. Since Yosef surely did not decompose, he asks again why Yosef said 'bring up my bones'.

title.en: Three partners: the bones come from the father

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Niddah that the father gives the bones and sinews and the mother the flesh and blood, warns that such statements of Chazal hold hidden meaning, and explains that the white bones carry chesed and so endure. He adds that a son inherits not as a relative but as the continuation of his father.

title.en: The answer: no part of Yaakov in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers all the questions: Yaakov's remains would stay in Mitzrayim through his sons, so Yosef promised more than he was asked and had his own bones, the part from his father, carried up, and commanded his brothers because honoring Yaakov is more on his sons than his grandsons. He explains the levels of distance that made Yaakov leave at once and Yosef wait for the geulah.

title.en: Every Jew carries something of Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from Rashi that every Jew, as an extension of Yaakov, will be brought to Eretz Yisrael through tunnels when Moshiach comes. He says that in a test a person should remind himself that a sin would cast a shadow on the kedushah of Yaakov, who stands for holiness.

title.en: Rebbi and Nebuchadnezzar: Torah is alive

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Rebbi cursed Nebuchadnezzar when teaching Megillas Esther but not when teaching Yirmiyah, since one may not curse a king. Since he was long dead in both cases, the Mashgiach concludes that learning Torah means reliving the moment it describes.

title.en: At the bedside of Yaakov and Yosef this Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Elisha's request for a double portion and the Chasam Sofer's regret at not being at his Rebbe's passing, and explains that one at a tzaddik's passing receives as much as his vessel holds. Since the Shabbos is woven of its parsha, this Shabbos Chazak one stands at the bedside of Yaakov and Yosef and can receive their blessings.

title.en: The night of the tekufah and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the coming night of Nittel: the shortest night, the tekufah, was a day of avodah zarah from Adam HaRishon's thanksgiving onward, and Chanukah, on the 25th like the 25 letters of Shema, brings light against it, which the other side imitates.

title.en: Two tekufos and the name Nittel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the two tekufos, Shmuel's and Rav Adda's, and why the dates of the gentile calendars differ. He connects their new year to the eighth day of Chanukah and says that the gematria of 'Nittel' equals 'Chanukah', the opposing force, and that many do not learn on that night.

title.en: Time, place and soul; Shabbos Vayechi as fuel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from Sefer Yetzirah that time, place and soul mirror each other, so as there is a place where Torah is not learned there is such a time, and brings the Gemara in Gittin. Chanukah and the kedushah of Shabbos Vayechi carry a Jew through that night, and he notes that time is holier than place and that customs differ.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the frog, a creature of both land and sea, is a mixture of pure and impure, and that its quiet song 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso' shows Hashem's kingship reaching even the places of tumah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Perek Shirah and the frog that told David HaMelech it sings more than he does, and asks what makes the frog's song so great. He brings Rashi and the Gemara on the words 'the frog came up': Rabbi Akiva says one frog multiplied, while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says one frog whistled and the rest gathered. Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the frog plague struck Egypt's yesod, measure for measure for Pharaoh's decree that aimed to mix the Jewish daughters with Egypt. The frog, which lives on land and in the sea, is a mixture of tahor and tamei, the very root of tumah. Through the Nefesh HaChaim's two kinds of unity he shows that the frog's song, 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso' said quietly, reveals Hashem's kingship even in impure places, and that tumah is bound to the number two. He closes with the Shovavim weeks, the signs of Moshiach, and the call for those who fear Hashem to bond together.

en: According to the Bnei Yissaschar the ten plagues correspond to the ten sefiros, and the frog plague, the second, corresponds to yesod, so the frogs struck the Egyptians in their hidden places.
Pharaoh's decree to kill the boys and keep the girls alive aimed to mix kedushah with tumah, and a mixture of good and evil is worse than evil alone.
The frog belongs to both land and sea, and since what is tahor on land is tamei in the sea and the reverse, it is a mixture of tahor and tamei, the essence of tumah.
'Baruch shem kevod malchuso' expresses the lower unity, that Hashem's kingship reaches even places of tumah, and for that reason it is said quietly.
The frog's song in Perek Shirah is 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso', the one song that is not a passuk, the song that comes out of the places of tumah.
Tumah is tied to the number two, separation from the One, which is why the tractates of the gravest tumos, Ohalos and Negaim, open with the word 'shnayim'.
In a generation mixed like the frog, the Mashgiach says the way to stay close to Hashem is through 'Baruch shem' and through bonding with those who fear Hashem.

candidateTopics: Hashem's kingship in places of tumah
bonding with those who fear Hashem

title.en: Perek Shirah and the frog's boast to David

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Perek Shirah, the song all creation sings to Hashem, brings Rabbi Yaakov Emden's answer to how impure creatures can sing, and tells how a frog told David HaMelech that it sings more than he does. He ties the theme to the weeks of the parshiyos of Yetzias Mitzrayim.

title.en: One frog: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the frog's song is praised, then brings Rashi on 'the frog came up' in the singular and the Gemara in Sanhedrin: Rabbi Akiva says one frog multiplied, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya sends him to Negaim and Ohalos and says one frog whistled and the rest came. He asks what bothered Rabbi Elazar and why he chose those tractates.

title.en: The frog plague and the middah of yesod

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the ten plagues match the ten sefiros, so that the frog plague matches yesod. He explains yesod as the power of bearing children and guarding the bris, and brings the Midrash that the frogs struck the Egyptians in their hidden places.

title.en: Pharaoh's decree: mixing good and evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pharaoh kept the girls alive to mix Jewish kedushah with Egypt, and that a mixture of good and evil is worse than evil alone, since tumah lives only off kedushah. He traces this to the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, applies it to the present generation with an example of a couple, and shows that the destruction and the Greek exile came through Jews who mixed.

title.en: Land and sea: the frog as a mixture

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the rule that everything on land has a counterpart in the sea, and that what is tahor on land is tamei in the sea and the reverse. Since the frog lives on both, it holds both, a mixture of tahor and tamei and the essence of tumah, and so it was the fitting punishment for Egypt's decree of mixing.

title.en: Baruch shem: the lower unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Yaakov's sons answered with Shema and he with 'Baruch shem', which is said quietly like the king's daughter's craving. Using the Nefesh HaChaim he explains Shema as the upper unity, all nullified to Hashem, and 'Baruch shem' as the lower unity, His kingship reaching even impure places, and adds the Tanya and Bilam.

title.en: The dog's song and the sea-dog

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Perek Shirah that Rabbi Yeshaya fasted 85 fasts to learn why dogs merit to sing, and was answered that it is because no dog moved its tongue in Egypt. He brings the Maharal that the dog is lowly because it is wholly nullified to its master, explains its song as the future tikun, asks why the dog was singled out, and brings the Mishnah in Keilim on the sea-dog.

title.en: Who sings for the impure: the frog's quiet song

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each impure species has a pure counterpart in land or sea that sings for it, but the dog has none, so it merits song only through its tongue. The frog has none either, and its song, the last in Perek Shirah, is 'Baruch shem' said quietly, the only song that is not a passuk, the song that comes from the places of tumah.

title.en: Tumah and the number two

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the mazikim flee when a Jew says Shema and quietly say 'Baruch shem', and that the second day of creation brought machlokes and Gehinnom. He shows that two means separation from the One, through zugos, Yeravam's two calves, hotza'ah on Shabbos, the Mishnayos that open with 'shtayim', and the Rambam's order of Seder Taharos, where Ohalos and Negaim open with 'shnayim'.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar's answer and the whistle of the shuruk

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Gemara: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya points Rabbi Akiva to Negaim and Ohalos, which open with 'shnayim', because tumah cannot begin from one root; yet two frogs would be pure tumah, so the frog plague was a partnership of one and many. He brings the passuk in Zechariah and the Metzudos on 'eshreka', connecting the whistle to the shuruk and kibbutz and to yesod.

title.en: The Shovavim weeks: tikun through Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the weeks of the parshiyos of Yetzias Mitzrayim are a time to repair yesod. Since this generation is too weak for fasts and afflictions, he says the tikun is toil in Torah and tzedakah, and tells of Rabbi Chatzkel of Kuzmir answering someone who asked how many fasts to take.

title.en: Moshiach is in the air

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the whole world is talking about Moshiach and sees this as a sign. He lists signs from Chazal, kingdoms provoking each other and the fear of sin being despised, and tells of a survivor in Detroit who was called 'crazy frum' for keeping Shabbos.

title.en: Preparing for Moshiach in a generation of frogs

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Malachi's counsel that those who fear Hashem should speak with one another, and says one must prepare to greet Moshiach. He explains 'vayishu b'divrei sheker', says hoping for Moshiach is a mitzvah, calls this a world of the frog where good and evil are mixed, and urges accepting not to spoil further, bringing the Tiferes Shlomo on loving Hashem even without desire.

title.en: Baruch shem: our song in the last generations

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Yaakov rejoicing that even the lowest generations say Shema and 'Baruch shem', and to the counsel to gather and bond with better people. He brings that the letters of 'Baruch shem' are the ones that combine with Hashem's Name, calls it the song of this mixed generation, and ends with the Midrash that only the frogs that jumped into the fire survived.

catalogTitle: דרוש נפלא במכת ברד - מכה של מלכות שמים (התעוררות לשובבים)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the plague of hail was a plague of malchus shamayim, and that Moshe Rabbeinu stopped it in the middle so that its yiras shamayim would stay suspended for the Jews in the war of Gog uMagog before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the shovavim weeks, when the parshiyos of yetzias Mitzrayim are read, and with Rosh Chodesh Shevat as a time of new Torah. Following the Ramban's count, the hail was announced in Shevat, and the Chasam Sofer ties it to Moshe beginning to explain the Torah in Shevat. He then raises a chain of questions: why 'he who feared the word of Hashem' appears only by the hail, how such Egyptians later chased the Jews, why Moshe left the city and spread his hands to stop this plague, and why Rashi calls it equal to all the plagues. After describing the war of Gog uMagog as a war against emunah, he shows that the hail, the seventh plague, corresponds to Shabbos and malchus shamayim. Moshe stopped it, and prayed that the rest stay suspended as yiras shamayim for the Jews before Moshiach. He closes with a call to use the weeks of shovavim.

en: Rosh Chodesh Shevat brings new Torah and a new conduct of the world, and the great people of the generation already feel it then.
The plague of hail corresponds to 'Remember the Shabbos day' and is a plague of malchus shamayim: a healing for the Jews and a blow for the Egyptians who rebelled against it.
Only someone who breaks his own nature to follow the tzaddik's advice is called 'one who fears the word of Hashem'.
Had the hail come down in full, the Egyptians would have submitted completely and the redemption would have come; because Moshe stopped it, their fear of Hashem was only temporary.
Moshe's prayer to stop the hail was for the Jews: that the rest of it stay suspended as yiras shamayim for the war of Gog uMagog before Moshiach.
The war of Gog uMagog is a war against emunah, in which the whole world is filled with heresy and even sincere Jews must struggle against doubts.

title.en: Shovavim and the renewal of Rosh Chodesh Shevat

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kotzker Rebbe on the parshiyos of yetzias Mitzrayim in the shovavim weeks, then explains through the Chiddushei HaRim why Beis Shammai place the new year for trees on Rosh Chodesh Shevat: then new Torah comes down, as Moshe began explaining the Torah on that day, and every person is judged on his connection to it.

title.en: The hail in the month of Shevat

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Hashem lifted Moshe above the heavens to bring the hail, and the Ramban's count that the warning of the hail fell in Shevat. Through the Chasam Sofer he links the suspended hail and the 'rain of Torah' in it to Moshe's explaining of the Torah in Shevat, and through the Zohar explains that the plagues were a healing for the Jews.

title.en: Why 'he who feared Hashem' appears only by the hail

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah mentions Egyptians who feared the word of Hashem only by the hail, although Rashi shows that some already saved their animals at the plague of pestilence. He answers that at the hail Moshe gave explicit advice to bring the animals in, and only those who could bring themselves to obey the tzaddik earn the title.

title.en: More questions on the hail

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the Egyptians the Torah calls God-fearing could supply Pharaoh's horses to chase the Jews, why Moshe had to leave the city and spread his hands to pray for the hail to stop, and why Rashi says the hail equals all the plagues. He brings the Midrash that the hail Moshe stopped hangs between heaven and earth until the war of Gog uMagog.

title.en: The war of Gog uMagog: a war against emunah

summary.en: As a first introduction the Mashgiach explains the war of Gog uMagog from Tehillim chapter two: a revolt against Hashem and His Moshiach, kingdoms built on heresy. Tzaddikim said it is a war against emunah that fills the world with doubts, and he explains why Ashrei ha'ish and Lamah ragshu count as one chapter: one prepares for this war by keeping away from scoffers.

title.en: A world of troubles and the coming Shabbos

summary.en: In a second introduction the Mashgiach explains that this world is full of suffering and only one who trusts Hashem has some happiness; it was not made for the Jews, so a salvation for a Jew is hard while one for a goy is easy. When Moshiach comes the world will become Shabbos, whose essence is malchus, the seventh of the middos, like the seventh month of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Hail corresponds to 'Remember the Shabbos day'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim that the ten plagues correspond to the ten commandments, and pairs them from the top: bechoros with Anochi, darkness with the second, and hail, the seventh plague, with Shabbos. With the Chasam Sofer's Shevat-Shabbos link he concludes that the hail broke the rebellion against malchus shamayim, a blow to the Egyptians and a delight to the Jews who rejoice in it.

title.en: Pharaoh submits and yiras shamayim rains down

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that at the hail, more than any earlier plague, Pharaoh submitted and said 'Hashem is righteous', because the hail rained malchus and yiras shamayim, so that even Egyptians feared Hashem. He compares it to the fear of Heaven that comes before Shabbos, with the story of Rebbe Reb Elimelech's town on erev Shabbos.

title.en: The interrupted hail and a passing fear

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that had the hail come down in full, the Egyptians would have submitted completely and all the plagues would have come at once; this is why Moshe's warning said 'all My plagues'. Because Pharaoh begged and Moshe stopped it, their fear of Hashem lasted only while the hail fell, as Moshe told Pharaoh, 'I know that you do not yet fear'.

title.en: Today's war and this year's opportunity

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the war of Gog uMagog is now, with no great tzaddikim to show Hashem as in earlier generations, and brings Malachi's last prophecy, read when Shabbos falls on erev Pesach as it does this year. He cites the Gemara and the Imrei Noam that this year is a special time for Moshiach, and urges joining tzaddikim and good friends, hearing words of yiras shamayim, and keeping the easy segulos of the Sefer Charedim.

title.en: Moshe's prayer was for the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe did not pray to stop the hail for Pharaoh but for the Jews: that part of the hail stay suspended as yiras shamayim for the time of Gog uMagog. Such a prayer meets many accusers, unlike a salvation for a goy, so he had to leave the city and spread out all ten fingers with all his powers. Alternatively, a full hail would have brought the days of Moshiach at once.

title.en: 'Hashem will reign', because Pharaoh's horse came

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Midrash in Yalkut Shimoni that the Jews said 'Hashem will reign' because 'Pharaoh's horse came', together with the Midrash that 'will reign' rather than 'reigns' showed that exile would still come. The horses that chased the Jews came from the God-fearing Egyptians whose animals the hail spared, a sign that the hail had not come down in full and the time of redemption had not yet arrived.

title.en: Shevat, shovavim and a call to use the time

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Rosh Chodesh Shevat: Moshe's explaining of the Torah, read on Shabbos Chazon and a sign of exile according to Rashi, carries the salvation hidden in the hail, just as half of leil shimurim was kept for Moshiach. He says these weeks bring yiras shamayim and softening of Jewish hearts, cites the Gerrer Rebbe on the wave of teshuvah and the Bnei Yissaschar on the call 'Return, wayward children', and closes with a plea not to waste the time and a brachah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef, raised from a shevet to one of the seven shepherds, embodies the kedushah of yesod and Seder Taharos, and that this is the heritage Sefer Bereishis leaves for the six weeks of Shovavim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by taking leave of Sefer Bereishis, whose root is the bris of Avraham Avinu. Of the seven shepherds, the Ushpizin, Yosef is the sixth, the midah of yesod and kedushas habris, praised by Yaakov as one who guarded his eyes. Since the sefer ends with Yosef's passing, Shovavim follows to repair this midah. The Mashgiach then asks how Rashi's two readings of 'yesh shever b'Mitzrayim', food and hope, share one root, and why the Baal HaTurim's acronym for 'zekunim' omits Taharos. He answers that each shepherd knew by himself the seder of Mishnah that shares his soul's root; Avraham, the first, knew all. Yosef knew Taharos by himself. Since taharah gives produce taste and fragrance, Yaakov tasted the grain Yosef distributed and sensed that Yosef was alive. The Mashgiach contrasts the Yishmaelim, closes on today's nisyonos, and says Torah and tefillah bring the geulah.

en: Each of the seven shepherds feeds all of Klal Yisrael with his midah; Yosef, the sixth, gives the kedushah of yesod and of the bris, which kept the Jews holy in Mitzrayim.
Because Sefer Bereishis ends with Yosef's passing, the six weeks of Shovavim begin right after it, to carry on and improve in Yosef's midah.
Each shepherd knew by himself the seder of Mishnah that comes from the same root as his soul, while Avraham, as the first, contained and knew them all.
Yosef knew Seder Taharos by himself, so Yaakov taught him only five sedarim, and the taste and fragrance of the grain he handled told Yaakov that Yosef was alive in Mitzrayim.
Today's generation faces nisyonos as hard as those at the beginning, and the Mashgiach says the counsel is Torah and tefillah, through which the geulah can be brought.

candidateTopics: Yosef and the midah of yesod

title.en: Yosef, the sixth shepherd, and Shovavim

summary.en: Taking leave of Sefer Bereishis, the Mashgiach explains that its root is the bris of Avraham, and that Yosef, the sixth of the seven shepherds, holds the midah of yesod. He brings the Alshich on 'ben poras Yosef', based on the Midrash that Yosef would not look at the women on the rooftops, and explains that Shovavim follows the sefer's close to repair this midah.

title.en: Food or hope in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's two readings of 'yesh shever b'Mitzrayim', that there is food and that there is hope, and sets out to find their common root. He adds the Targum Yonasan that merchants brought grain, and Rashi and the Baal HaTurim on 'ben zekunim': Yaakov taught Yosef the Torah of Shem and Ever, the sedarim Zeraim, Kodashim, Nashim, Yeshuos and Moed.

title.en: Where is Taharos, and why did Yaakov learn?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the acronym lacks Seder Taharos, and why Yaakov did not teach the other shevatim. He brings that Avraham knew the whole Torah by himself through his attachment to Hashem, and asks why Yaakov, the choicest of the Avos, had to learn from Shem and Ever or from Avraham and Yitzchak.

title.en: Shepherds above shevatim; the days and the sedarim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven shepherds feed all of Klal Yisrael while each shevet serves only his own tribe; Yosef was raised to a shepherd and his sons became shevatim, and his kedushah kept the Jews pure in Mitzrayim. He then explains the Chok LeYisrael order, after the Arizal, in which each day of the week corresponds to a shepherd and a seder of Mishnah.

title.en: Each shepherd knew his own seder

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that each shepherd knew by himself the seder that shares his soul's root: Zeraim is Avraham, Moed Yitzchak, Nashim Yaakov. Bringing the Zohar that 'six days' means six midos, he explains that the first midah contains all, so Avraham knew everything, while Yaakov knew only Nashim by himself. Yosef, raised to a shepherd, knew Taharos by himself, which is why Yaakov taught him only five sedarim and loved him.

title.en: Taharah, taste and fragrance

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Sotah that when taharah ceased, the taste and fragrance of fruit ceased. Yosef personally oversaw the planting and distribution of grain, and his power entered it, so the grain had a wondrous taste and fragrance; tasting it, Yaakov sensed that Yosef was alive. Thus Rashi's two readings are one, and he notes that 'yesh shever b'Mitzrayim' equals 'Seder Taharos' in gematria.

title.en: Yishmael, the opposite of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that of ten measures of immorality, Arabia took nine, and explains that the Yishmaelim are the opposite of Yosef, covering their impurity with an outward show of tznius, and that Rashi says they usually carried foul-smelling goods, yet with Yosef they carried spices. 'Ki ben zekunim hu' equals 'ta'am reyach', and the Gemara in Berachos says that pure bachurim will give off fragrance.

title.en: The nisyonos of today's world

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how much more modest the streets were when he was young, recalling separate school doors for boys and girls, and how the permissive Western culture has made the world one big place of immorality, through radio, television and the internet. He brings the Gemara about a father who perfumes his son and sets him at the door of a house of ill repute.

title.en: Torah and tefillah bring the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the end is a replay of the beginning, so the last generation faces nisyonos like Avraham's, yet Hashem does not give tests that are too hard. He speaks of the bachurim of today and says the counsel is Torah and tefillah; as Yosef's passing ushers in Shovavim and 'Chazak', everyone is a shaliach to bring the geulah, and there is hope in today's Mitzrayim.

catalogTitle: “החודש הזה לכם” - התחדשות הלבנה' אילנות בשבט' וכנ"י

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Klal Yisrael identifies with the renewed moon and the reviving tree of Shevat, because they are the 'reishis' of the world, and that the whole Torah from Bereishis to 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem' answers why only they can be trusted with Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rosh Chodesh Shevat, when Moshe began explaining the Torah, as a time of renewal. The tree that seems dead all winter and the moon that disappears are two witnesses that Klal Yisrael, which identifies with both, will be renewed from a tiny point that never vanishes; Beis Shammai, who belong to the world of Moshiach, sense that point already on the first of Shevat. Each mitzvah is a tree, trees daven together with a person, and on Tu BiShvat one can pray that barren trees, and barren Jews, bear fruit. Klal Yisrael is the 'reishis' of the world. He explains why the Mishnah states Beis Shammai's view first, and why 'HaChodesh' is the first mitzvah. The Torah has three parts: the Torah of creation, of man, and of Yisrael. Man's choice can build or ruin nature, within a built-in limit; control passed to Avraham's family, and Eretz Yisrael, the root of the world, can be trusted only to the nation that is 'reishis'.

en: The tree that revives in Shevat and the renewed moon are two witnesses that Klal Yisrael, which identifies with them, will be renewed even when the nations think it is dead.
Every Jew has a small point that can never be nullified, and from that point his salvation and that of all Klal Yisrael will spread.
Klal Yisrael is the 'reishis', the beginning from which the whole world develops, and the first mitzvah given to them, 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem', is itself about a beginning.

The Torah has three parts: the Torah of creation, which nature obeys without choice; the Torah of man, the seven Noahide mitzvos, given with free choice; and the Torah of Yisrael, beginning with 'HaChodesh'.
Because man is part of nature, his choice can repair or ruin all of nature, but the Creator built a control system into the world that sets a limit to how far it can be ruined.
Since Avraham, control of the world was taken from the nations and given to his children, and Eretz Yisrael, the root of the world, can be trusted only to the nation that is 'reishis'.
