free will and its effect on nature
Eretz Yisrael as the root of the world
the nations' claim to Eretz Yisrael

title.en: Shevat: the reviving tree and the renewed moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rosh Chodesh Shevat, when Moshe began explaining the Torah, as a time of renewal, and with the Mishnah's dispute over the new year for trees. He describes the tree that seems dead all winter and then revives, and the moon that symbolizes the kingdom of Yisrael, and says both bear witness that Klal Yisrael will be renewed from a small point.

title.en: Beis Shammai and the point that never vanishes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Beis Shammai belong to the world of Moshiach and therefore sense the renewal already on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, when it is only a point. He says every Jew, even one who feels no taste in learning or davening, has a small point that can never be nullified, from which his salvation will grow.

title.en: Man is a tree: mitzvos, prayer and judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings 'ki ha'adam etz hasadeh' and 'kimei ha'etz yemei ami': each mitzvah is a tree that grows from a seed. He explains that the trees of the field daven together with a person, and that according to the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov Tu BiShvat is the day of judgment for the trees, including the trees that are Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Praying for the barren trees

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that when Moshiach comes even barren trees will bear fruit, since they are barren only because of the curse on the ground after Adam's sin. On Tu BiShvat, the day of judgment of the trees, one can join their prayer and daven that every barren tree bear fruit.

title.en: The Jew who feels like a barren tree

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a Jew who feels he has the power to learn, daven and do chesed but is frozen like a dead tree, and says he can join the trees' minyan on Tu BiShvat. The fruits may be spiritual: he brings what is said of the Ohr HaChaim, and links the end of the Torah with the start of Moshe's explanation of the Torah on Rosh Chodesh Shevat.

title.en: Klal Yisrael as the 'reishis' of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Klal Yisrael, the Torah and Eretz Yisrael are each called 'reishis', the beginning from which the world develops, and that Yisrael is Hashem's firstborn. Pharaoh refused to acknowledge this and was struck in his firstborn; Esav too disputed Yaakov's hidden birthright, and the first mitzvah, about the moon, reveals who the 'reishis' is.

title.en: Why the Mishnah states Beis Shammai first

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Mishnah on the new year for trees states Beis Shammai's view as the main statement, unlike everywhere else. He answers that in the days of Moshiach the halacha will follow Beis Shammai, and since Moshiach may come before the fruit is tithed, a Jew who awaits him must know already now which fruit blossomed before Rosh Chodesh Shevat.

title.en: 'HaChodesh' as the first mitzvah and the Sinai foundation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's opening question why the Torah does not begin with 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem', the first mitzvah, and asks how it is first when milah was commanded earlier. From the Rambam he explains that our emunah rests on the whole nation witnessing Sinai, not on a prophet's signs, so we keep earlier mitzvos only because Moshe commanded them, and 'HaChodesh' is the first mitzvah given to Yisrael.

title.en: The Torah of creation and the limits of miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the first part of the Torah is the Torah of creation: grass grows and birds fly because the Torah commands it, just as a Jew puts on tzitzis. Therefore tzaddikim avoided miracles, which change what the Torah set; he illustrates with Reb Chaim Ozer's advice to a sick man to move to Eretz Yisrael, and with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, explaining that a miracle must stay within the Torah's own rules.

title.en: Three parts of the Torah and man's choice

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces the Torah of creation from Bereishis to the rivers of Gan Eden, then the Torah of man from 'vayetzav' with the seven Noahide mitzvos, then the Torah of Yisrael from 'HaChodesh'. Creation has no choice, while man does, and since man is part of nature his choice extends to all of nature, as the giant fruit seen by the spies showed.

title.en: Man can ruin nature, within a built-in limit

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how man's sins forced nature to sin with him: Adam's sin brought thorns, and the generation of the Flood corrupted even animals and stopped the luminaries. Yet man is a microcosm with a built-in control system, like an upset stomach or a fever fighting germs, and history and the Flood show that the world has a limit beyond which it cannot be ruined.

title.en: From Adam to Avraham: the key to the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'le'ovdah uleshomrah' as positive and negative mitzvos through which man builds or ruins the world. Following the Derech Hashem, he explains that after Adam, the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion corrupted nature, Hashem took control from mankind and gave it to Avraham's family, offered the Torah once more to the nations, and gave it to Yisrael when their very reality refused it.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, root of the world, and the nations' claim

summary.en: Using the Sefer Yetzirah's world, time and soul, the Mashgiach explains that Eretz Yisrael is the 'Noach' among places, untouched by the Flood, the 'reishis' from which the world spread. He then asks what the nations' claim 'you are bandits' means, when conquest normally acquires land, and answers that driving a nation out of the root of the world is like driving it off the planet, which is why they demand that Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim be international.

title.en: Rashi's answer to the nations and the bikkurim of 'reishis'

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents Rashi's answer to the nations: the Torah's story from creation shows control passing from Adam to Avraham's perfected descendants, and Eretz Yisrael, where a mitzvah or sin has the greatest effect, can be trusted only to a purified holy nation. He closes with the Haggadah's 'arami oved avi', the bikkurim passuk, showing that the Jew who knows he is 'reishis', in the land of 'reishis', brings the first fruits, at a time when the redemption begins to sprout from the small point.

catalogTitle: הדרכה וחיזוק לדור של הסתר פנים: "אהבתי אתכם אמר ה'"

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the darkness before Moshiach is like the plague of darkness in Egypt, and that a broken generation is strengthened above all by hearing Malachi's opening words, 'I have loved you, says Hashem'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that the name of a parsha carries its content, and that the souls of the recent generations, purified by their suffering, are being prepared for Moshiach. He links the ten makkos to the ten sefiros, with makas bechoros against keser, and teaches that every Jew holds a point of 'bechor', a first beginning, from which he can always start anew. He then reads David HaMelech's verse 'He sent darkness... and they did not rebel against His word' with the Chasam Sofer: during choshech the Jews could have fled, yet they waited for Moshe, while four fifths of the people, those who did not want to leave, died. Our time before Moshiach is such a darkness. Contrasting Yeshayahu's rebuke with Malachi, who spoke to a broken people, the Mashgiach shows that this generation must hear 'Ahavti eschem', learn sefarim of Hashem's love, never be cooled off, and always begin again: 'Bo', Hashem goes with a Jew everywhere.

en: Each of the ten makkos corresponds to one of the ten sefiros, and makas bechoros, at the end of parshas Bo, corresponds to keser, the root.
Every Jew has within him a point of 'bechor', a first beginning, and through the power of yetzias Mitzrayim he can always begin anew.
During the plague of darkness the Jews obeyed Moshe and waited, although four fifths of the people died; this was a test of great emunah.
The time before Moshiach is a darkness like makas choshech, in which those who serve Hashem feel no encouragement.
Malachi, speaking to a broken generation, opens with 'Ahavti eschem', and a generation like ours must be strengthened by learning how much Hashem loves every Jew.
The word 'Bo', come, teaches that Hashem goes along with a Jew everywhere, and no darkness can separate him from Hashem.

title.en: Souls returning to be prepared for Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that a parsha's name holds its content. He brings that the generation of the flood came back in Egypt and was drowned in the Nile measure for measure, and suggests that the souls killed al kiddush Hashem are now being reborn, purified, as better children for the generation of Moshiach.

title.en: The makkos and the sefiros; reading the parsha of geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ten makkos stand against the ten sefiros, with makas bechoros against keser, and that Bo holds the highest ones. Because the parsha is about the geulah, reading and learning it with kavanah can awaken redemption, at least a personal one, and he urges constant talk of Moshiach.

title.en: Tu BiShvat and the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel over the new year for trees and the separation of tithes from old and new fruit, and connects Tu BiShvat, which always falls in the weeks of the geulah parshiyos, with keeping the geulah in mind.

title.en: Remembering yetzias Mitzrayim as the source of every yeshuah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one must believe that learning the parsha draws down makkos on the enemies of Israel and yeshuos for Jews. Remembering yetzias Mitzrayim is the source of all Jewish salvations, which is why Shabbos Kiddush recalls it as a new beginning.

title.en: The point of 'bechor' and the power to begin again

summary.en: From makas bechoros, which revealed 'Bni bechori Yisrael', the Mashgiach teaches that every Jew holds a point of first beginning that he can always rekindle. Hashem gave the mitzvah of 'Hachodesh hazeh' together with yetzias Mitzrayim, in the spring, so that a Jew can start over even a hundred times, and the daily mention of yetzias Mitzrayim gives that power.

title.en: The darkness before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one can draw from Pesach and from parshas Bo the power to leave one's own Egypt. As in Egypt, before Moshiach comes an unprecedented darkness, which the sefarim foretold, and the destruction this generation saw had no equal.

title.en: 'They did not rebel against His word'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why David HaMelech lists choshech first among the makkos, and brings the Chasam Sofer: during the darkness the paralyzed Egyptians could not stop the Jews, yet the Jews waited because Moshe told them to. He contrasts the bnei Efrayim who left Egypt early on their own and fell to the Pelishtim, which is why Hashem did not lead the people by the land of the Pelishtim.

title.en: Who died in the darkness, and why

summary.en: Bringing Rashi that only one in five left Egypt, the Mashgiach explains that those who died were the wealthy and the 'intelligentsia' close to the government, who did not want to leave. The dilemma of staying or going had one answer, to follow Moshe; the bnei Efrayim failed because they did not even ask Amram, the leader of the generation, and lacked emunas chachamim.

title.en: Picturing the plague of darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks the listeners to picture Egypt during choshech: by the smallest count in the Midrash, eighty percent of the Jews died, and every home lost a brother, a father or a child. The survivors needed tremendous emunah to keep following Moshe, and that is the meaning of 'He sent darkness': it was dark for the Jews too, yet they did not rebel.

title.en: Today's test: serving Hashem without feeling

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the test of today: a Jew learns and davens and feels nothing, while those who use crooked means succeed. This is no surprise but the plan foretold by Malachi, the last prophet, who speaks of the period before Moshiach, when people say serving Hashem brings no gain, and of the day when the difference between the one who serves Hashem and the one who does not will be seen.

title.en: Yeshayahu's rebuke and Malachi's 'Ahavti eschem'

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in such a time one must learn sefarim that strengthen, not ones that dwell on punishment. Yeshayahu opened his prophecy with harsh rebuke because he spoke to a generation on a high level, but Malachi spoke to broken Jews who had seen destruction and asked questions, so he opens with 'Ahavti eschem amar Hashem'.

title.en: Chazal on Hashem's love for the simplest Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a chain of Chazal on Hashem's love: Yaakov's garments smelled sweet even through the 'bogdim', the traitors; Bilam saw the mitzvos of the lowest Jew; even the empty ones are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate. He then explains the Midrash on 'the crown his mother made him': Hashem calls Klal Yisrael daughter, sister and even mother out of love, and the Torah and mitzvos of Jews become His crown.

title.en: Not letting oneself be cooled off

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in the darkness a Jew must hear Malachi's words from over two thousand years ago, which accompany us until his last verse about Eliyahu. One must not let the yetzer hara cool him off by pointing to friends who took another road and became successful, or by saying Hashem does not want his mitzvos; a Jew who feels no life in davening or Shabbos must know that Hashem loves him and that this is the plan.

title.en: 'Bo el Paroh': Hashem goes along

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem tells Moshe 'Bo', come, to Pharaoh, and explains that Hashem goes with him: nothing can separate a Jew from Hashem, even in Pharaoh's palace full of idols, like a mother who goes with her small child into a dark room. He brings David HaMelech's words that Hashem is in the heavens and in the depths and that darkness does not darken before Him, and concludes that after any fall a Jew can begin now, as in the renewal of the spring.

title.en: Yehudah begins anew; never losing courage

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Yehudah married right after the sale of Yosef: seeing he had lost everything, he began from the beginning, and the first mitzvos of the Torah teach the same renewal. He brings Rashi that Hashem took the Jews out of Egypt for what they would become, tells a story from the Yesod HaAvodah of a general told that losing courage is worse than losing a fortress, and closes: Bo, come to Hashem; nothing can separate a Jew from Him.

catalogTitle: חוט הזהב של פרשה זו - אמונה (שער הבטחון של חובות הלבבות)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that emunah is the golden thread running through Parshas Beshalach, and through the Chovos HaLevavos' distinctions between one who trusts in Hashem and one who does not, he explains how bitachon shapes a person's view of mazal, parnassah and the trials of life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by tracing emunah through the parsha: the Midrash on 'vayaseiv' teaches leaning on Hashem, and the Song at the Sea flows from 'vaya'aminu', because only one who is content with Hashem's ways can sing. Linking the week to Tu Bishvat, he reads Yirmiyahu's two trees, the one who trusts in man and the one who trusts in Hashem, and urges learning Shaar HaBitachon. He then goes through its distinctions: the one who trusts is content with both good and bad, has peace of mind, and works without relying on the means. Along the way he explains mazal, why a tzaddik may be poor, and the manna as the lesson that each receives exactly his portion. He warns against careers that endanger the soul and against questionable earnings, tells stories of Reb Zusha, Rabbi Yisrael Salanter and the Ba'al Shem Tov, and closes with the Jewish tree that must be transplanted to its own soil.

en: Emunah is the thread that runs through the whole parsha, from the Exodus through the Song at the Sea, the manna and Amalek.
Shirah is the expression of contentment, and only one who trusts that Hashem controls everything can sing.
True bitachon is not the belief that Hashem will give one everything one wants, but being content with whatever Hashem does, knowing it is for one's good.
A person's mazal is the channel through which his flow of blessing comes, and Hashem places each soul in the mazal it needs for its tikkun.
The manna teaches that each person receives exactly his portion, whether he toils for it or not.
One works because Hashem wants the world settled, not because the work brings the parnassah, so one must never compromise on Yiddishkeit or honesty for a living.

title.en: Emunah, the thread of the parsha

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how emunah runs through Beshalach, from the Midrash on 'vayaseiv' that teaches leaning on Hashem to the Song at the Sea. He explains shirah as contentment, tells of the Chasam Sofer teaching his son to live with a question, and ties the custom of kasha on Shabbos Shirah to swallowing a kushya.

title.en: Tu Bishvat and Yirmiyahu's two trees

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the week to Tu Bishvat, when each person, a branch of the great tree, should ask which tree he belongs to. He reads Yirmiyahu's contrast between the dry shrub of one who trusts in man and the tree by the water of one who trusts in Hashem, and urges learning a chapter of Shaar HaBitachon this week.

title.en: First distinction: content with good and bad

summary.en: Bringing the Chovos HaLevavos, the Mashgiach explains that one who trusts is content with whatever Hashem does and thanks Him for bad as for good, like Dovid's 'chesed umishpat ashirah', while one who does not trust credits himself for good and grows angry at bad. He stresses that bitachon is not the belief that one will get everything one wants.

title.en: Reb Zusha and the higher kind of person

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Maggid sent a suffering man to Reb Zusha, who did not know why he was sent since he lacked nothing, and compares bitachon to a child who trusts his father. He adds that one close to Hashem is usually granted more kindness and senses salvation, and brings sayings of the Sanzer Rav and the Kotzker that this world is not what counts.

title.en: Second distinction: peace of mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the second distinction: one who trusts has peace of mind, knowing Hashem acts for his good, while one who does not trust has no rest even when things go well, always worrying about tomorrow. He reads the Chovos HaLevavos that Hashem brought each person into the world at a set time and withholds parnassah until its set time.

title.en: Mazal and why a tzaddik may be poor

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara that the angel declares at conception whether one will be wise or foolish, rich or poor, but not righteous or wicked, and that mazal means a channel of flow. He asks why a lucky person succeeds more than a great tzaddik and answers that above mazal Hashem has accounts from earlier gilgulim and generations, citing Rabbi Akiva on why the poor are poor.

title.en: Exactly measured: the nursing child and the manna

summary.en: Following the Chovos HaLevavos, the Mashgiach says a person should tell himself that Hashem knows what his soul needs, as every creature was made with its own consent. He explains that Hashem fed him as an infant exactly what he needed each day, as with the manna, 'devar yom beyomo', and that Hashem chooses the place, the person and the way through which parnassah comes, all for one's good.

title.en: Sefer HaYashar: trials test the strong

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads a passage from Rabbeinu Tam's Sefer HaYashar: all the changes that come upon a person, good or bad, can distract him from serving Hashem, and they are the test of whether he is strong, unmoved like a mountain in the wind. One must prepare daily for trials, since the world is full of troubles, and then he remains b'simcha even in bad times.

title.en: Third distinction: means without reliance

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the third distinction: one who trusts engages in the means of parnassah without relying on them. He says the reason to work is that Hashem wants the world settled, which is why the Gemara disqualifies the dice player, and that while one may choose to devote himself entirely to Torah he cannot demand it. One should choose kosher work, and if the means fail he does not lose his trust.

title.en: A casualty rate for the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the fear of the Vietnam draft, with its casualty rate, to the danger a yeshiva bachur faces in preparing for parnassah in ways not fully in Hashem's path, which has its own casualty rate for the soul. Citing the Mesilas Yesharim that man was created for the World to Come, he says people guard against physical danger but not spiritual, because they lack emunah, and consoles that even Noach was of 'ketanei amanah'.

title.en: No questionable earnings; the manna at the door

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments that even fine Jews cut corners in parnassah, brings a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer on a product of doubtful kashrus, and says one with true emunah does not reach for earnings with a doubt. He gives the parable of a thirsty man who drinks bad water minutes before finding a pure spring, and explains 'shatu ha'am' about the manna: those who went far for it were foolish, since those who waited found it at their door.

title.en: Stories of the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rabbi Yisrael Salanter

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a Lithuanian story of a discussion in Vilna about how much bitachon one needs, and of the Ba'al Shem Tov, before he was revealed, knocking on a door when hungry and walking on without waiting. He then tells how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter needed a watch and one arrived through a Jewish soldier back from the war.

title.en: Not to the swift: ability is also mazal

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Koheles' 'lo lakalim hamerotz', illustrating with his own running for a bus and slipping. He explains that the energy and aggressiveness of successful businessmen are themselves part of the mazal the angel proclaimed, so one destined for wealth will become wealthy honestly, and it is foolish to run after it at the expense of avodas Hashem.

title.en: The jar of manna and Hashem's many messengers

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the jar of manna kept for the generations, which Yirmiyahu showed to those who would leave Torah to earn a living: Hashem has many messengers to bring a person's sustenance. He brings the Gemara that the Rabbanan learned the meaning of 'hashlech al Hashem yehavcha', and tells of a man who sat on a wagon yet kept his load on his shoulder.

title.en: Same omer for all; the Jewish tree transplanted

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes with the lesson that one who gathered manna all day and one who went out for minutes each had exactly an omer. He explains 'emunas' as Seder Zera'im, since the farmer believes in Hashem and sows, says that all Jews believe deep down, and ends with Tu Bishvat: the Jewish tree needs its own soil, and he prays that Hashem transplant the Jews, as 'tevi'emo vetita'emo' in this parsha.

catalogTitle: A Persons Name - the Handle of his נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's name is the handle of his neshama and the code of his mission in this world, and that Sefer Shemos, the book of names, is the book of geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Parshas Shemos with the idea that a name is the handle of the neshama, given to a child with a touch of ruach hakodesh, illustrated by stories of the Chozeh of Lublin and Rabbi Shlomo of Radomsk. Through the Bnei Yissaschar he explains that Pharaoh first took away the midwives' Jewish names so they would fall under tumah, and only then ordered them to kill. The Gemara in Berachos, that names have an effect, leads him to the two meanings of shamos: devastation and astonishment. People cannot understand Hashem's ways; only the Zohar's revelation, that the Jews in Mitzrayim were the souls of the Mabul and Haflagah generations and Moshe was Noach, explains their suffering. Today no one can explain tragedies like the Holocaust, and the generation's test is to believe. Each name hides a mission, two equal names can differ like the combinations of Hashem's name in the months, and the names in Shemos are names of geulah. He ends with Shovavim as a time of teshuvah.

en: A Jew's name is the handle of his neshama: it is the name his soul was called in heaven, and a person responds to his name because he responds through his neshama.
Being called by one's Jewish name draws kedushah and reminds a person why he came down; Pharaoh therefore first forbade the midwives their Jewish names before ordering them to kill.
Human beings cannot understand Hashem's workings in the world; only a revelation such as the Zohar on the souls in Mitzrayim explains why suffering came.
In the generations before Moshiach Hashem is hidden and no one can explain tragedies such as the Holocaust; the test of this generation is to believe without understanding.
Every person's mission is encoded in his name; devastation can only be understood by knowing the names, that is the missions, of those who suffer it.
Two people with the same name can be entirely different, as the same four letters of Hashem's name in different orders give months of chesed or of din.
The names at the start of Shemos are not a repetition of Vayigash but names of geulah, and Sefer Shemos, the book of redemption, opens the six weeks of Shovavim, a time of teshuvah.

title.en: A name is the handle of the neshama

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first passuk of Shemos and explains that a name is the soul's heavenly name, given by a father with a touch of ruach hakodesh. He tells of the Chozeh of Lublin, of Rabbi Shlomo of Radomsk who found every Jew's name in Sefer Shemos, and of a hospital where doctors shouted a patient's name to test for a coma.

title.en: Why Pharaoh changed the midwives' names

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's question why the Torah says 'vayomer' twice to the midwives. He answers that the first command was to drop the names Yocheved and Miriam for Egyptian names, so that tumah would break their resistance; only then came the order to kill, and they disobeyed both.

title.en: The Gemara: a name has an effect

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that a name influences a person, with Rabbi Meir recognizing a wicked man by his name, and its proof from the passuk 'asher sam shamos ba'aretz', read as 'shemos'. He asks how this proves anything when the correct reading is shamos.

title.en: Shamos: devastation and astonishment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that shamos means both devastation and astonishment. Man understands Hashem's ways less than a fly understands a spaceship launch, yet people write books explaining history; had they lived in Mitzrayim they would have written that Hashem abandoned the Avos' children.

title.en: The souls of the Mabul and Haflagah in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the Jews in Mitzrayim were the souls of the Dor Haflagah, who built with clay and bricks, and of the Dor HaMabul, whose sons were thrown into the river. Moshe Rabbeinu was Noach, which explains the Gemara in Chullin that finds Moshe hinted in the parshah of the Mabul.

title.en: Mei Noach and Moshe's 'mecheini'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Navi calls the Flood 'the waters of Noach': Noach did not daven for his generation. Moshe rectified this when he said 'mecheini' after the eigel, a word whose letters form 'mei Noach', and like Noach he was saved in a teivah, by Basya.

title.en: Nothing is random; Hashem hidden today

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the suffering in Mitzrayim paid an old debt, and brings Chazal that the generation of the Churban were the souls of the eigel. Today, he says, Hashem is concealed as was foretold for the end of galus, and there are no tzaddikim to explain, though this changed only recently.

title.en: Tach v'Tat and the biryonim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the tzaddikim's explanation that the Jews killed in the gezeiros of Tach v'Tat were the souls of the biryonim of the second Churban, who, as the Gemara in Gittin tells, defied Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and caused needless bloodshed against the Romans.

title.en: Believing without explanations

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that today no one is qualified to explain, but the merit of believing without explanations is very great. After the Holocaust some wrote books asking whether G-d is dead, but the backbone of Klal Yisrael believes; when Moshiach comes we will understand, and each person has a mission hidden in his name.

title.en: The name as the code of a mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that an angel's name changes with its mission, and says a Jew's name is the code of his mission. Bereishis shows reward and punishment openly; Shemos opens with suffering and with names. This answers the Gemara: the devastation can only be understood through the names of those who undergo it.

title.en: Why repeat the names? Two Shimons

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the names of the Shevatim are repeated from Vayigash, and raises a difficulty: Shimon HaTzaddik and Shimon, the leader of the biryonim, bore the same name. Recalling boys who described movies with good guys and bad guys, he asks how one name can belong to either.

title.en: Male first in kedushah, female first in tumah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in lashon hakodesh the order of letters changes everything, as with the twelve combinations of Hashem's name for the months. The rule is that in kedushah the male, chesed, comes first, which is why the Shulchan Aruch puts the right shoe first, while in tumah the female comes first, as by Esav.

title.en: Nissan, Teves and the two Shimons

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that in Nissan's combination of Hashem's name the yud and vav precede the heh, while in Teves the heh comes first, making it a dark, cold month of din. So too two people named Shimon may have different arrangements: each has free choice to be a tzaddik or rasha, but not to change his essential traits.

title.en: Names of geulah and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the names in Vayigash speak of going into galus, while in Shemos, the Ramban's Sefer HaGeulah, the Midrash reads each Shevet's name as a name of redemption. He adds that a boy is named at the bris on the eighth day because the bris carries geulah, and that the last letters of 'Bnei Yisrael haba'im Mitzraymah' spell milah.

title.en: Sefer HaGeulah and Shovavim

summary.en: The Mashgiach follows the Ramban that Sefer Shemos, the book of redemption, climaxes with the Shechinah resting on the Mishkan. He brings 'shuvu banim shovavim' and the Arizal that Shovavim stands for the first six sedros of Shemos, from Yetzias Mitzrayim to Matan Torah, which make these six weeks a time of teshuvah, since the Torah is alive.

title.en: Using the weeks of Shovavim

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that earlier generations fasted during Shovavim and that the Bnei Yissaschar calls it a time of teshuvah and Tehillim. He does not advocate fasting today, but asks that one be aware of the season, learn the sedros and experience Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, mentioning a half hour of Tehillim before Shacharis on Fridays in his beis medrash.

catalogTitle: מה "הים ראה וינס"? "וינס ויצא החוצה." (ט"ו בשבט)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sea split on seeing Yosef's coffin because Yosef, who fled before he could lose his free choice, signals that the geulah is split in two and that Klal Yisrael, like a tree on Tu BiShvat, never truly dies.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah repeats in Beshalach that Moshe took Yosef's bones, and answers with the Midrash that the sea fled when it saw Yosef's coffin. The sea had a condition from creation to split for the complete geulah; when it sensed the final redemption had not yet come, it refused. Hashem divided the geulah in two, like yachatz, because the Jews stood at the forty-ninth gate of impurity. Yosef, whose name alludes to a second redemption, embodied this; and just as Yosef fled when he could no longer hold out, Hashem took the Jews out before they lost their free choice. The Mashgiach then explains why Yosef made his brothers swear to carry his bones, as an extension of honoring Yaakov. For Tu BiShvat he describes the tree whose life survives the winter in its roots: Klal Yisrael and every Jew never die. He closes by urging Jews to stay like the earlier fruits of the tree, following their fathers' ways.

en: The sea's condition from creation was to split for the complete geulah, so it first refused to split at the Exodus.
Hashem divided the geulah in two, like yachatz, keeping the larger half hidden for the final redemption, and Yosef's coffin showed the sea this division.
Just as Yosef fled when he could no longer withstand the test and was about to lose his free choice, Hashem took the Jews out of Egypt before they lost theirs at the forty-ninth gate of impurity.
No Jew, and not Klal Yisrael, can ever fall so low that he entirely loses his free choice and is lost.
Yosef asked to be buried in Eretz Yisrael as an extension of honoring Yaakov, since a son's bones are part of his father.
On Tu BiShvat the sap starts rising in the roots of a tree that looks dead, and this is the sign that Klal Yisrael, compared to a tree, never dies.
Jewish fruit must grow 'after its kind': the Mashgiach says the way to know who belongs to the tree is whether one follows the ways of one's fathers.

title.en: Why Yosef's bones appear in Beshalach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah repeats in Beshalach that Moshe took Yosef's bones, and answers that it belongs to the splitting of the sea, since the Midrash says the sea saw Yosef's coffin. He then asks why the sea needed the coffin at all, when it was created with a condition to split.

title.en: The sea's first condition and Yosef's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the sea returned 'to its first condition' and asks why that fits only when the sea closed again. He then brings the Midrash that the names of the tribes allude to the geulah, and that Yosef's name recalls Yeshaya's prophecy that Hashem will 'add a second time' His hand, with the Radak's explanation of a second redemption and a second splitting of the sea.

title.en: A geulah split in two, like yachatz

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that only Yosef's name speaks of a future redemption. He explains, following the Arizal, that the Jews were at the forty-ninth gate of impurity and could not stay longer, so the geulah was divided like yachatz: the smaller half came in Egypt and the greater half is hidden for Moshiach, when all of creation will sing.

title.en: Why the sea refused, and what it saw

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sea's condition was to split for the final redemption, so it sensed the time had not come and refused. Hashem told it He must split the geulah in two; the sea saw Yosef's coffin, a sign that the geulah is divided, and split. This explains why the Midrash says it returned to its first condition only when it closed: its condition is still to be fulfilled.

title.en: 'He fled and went outside': Yosef's test

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'the sea saw and fled' as the sea seeing how Yosef fled from his test. Yosef was a lone seventeen-year-old pressed daily for a whole year; when his strength gave out and he was about to lose his free choice, Hashem held him back and he fled. Measure for measure, Hashem took the Jews out before they lost their free choice at the forty-ninth gate, and the Mashgiach draws the promise that no Jew can fall that far.

title.en: Yaakov at the sea and Yosef's oath

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that 'Yisrael' who saw the great hand at the sea is Yaakov Avinu, and asks why Yaakov in particular. He then asks, on Rashi, why Yosef made his brothers rather than his sons swear to carry his bones, and why Yosef answered Yaakov's request not to be buried in Egypt with 'I will do as you say', which seems to lack respect.

title.en: A son's bones and honoring Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Yosef was called 'bones' in his lifetime for staying silent when his brothers said 'your servant our father'. He explains that a son is an extension of his father, so Yosef's bones were part of Yaakov; Yosef promised more than Yaakov asked, that his own bones too would not stay in Egypt, and charged his brothers, who were more obligated in Yaakov's honor than his own sons. Calling himself 'bones' stressed that his concern was only his father's honor, and he adds that a residue of the soul's life remains in the bones.

title.en: Tu BiShvat: life hidden in the roots

summary.en: Turning to Tu BiShvat, the Mashgiach explains the dispute whether the new year for trees is the first or fifteenth of Shevat: the sharper Beis Shammai sensed it earlier. He ties the weeks of reading about the plagues to the start of redemption, and describes how in Shevat the sap begins to move in the roots of a tree that looks dead under the snow, preparing for Nissan.

title.en: 'Like the days of a tree': Israel never dies

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the navi comparing the days of his people to the days of a tree. When the nations and even Jews declare the Jewish people dead, the tree on Tu BiShvat testifies that its life survives, and the bracha on fruit thanks Hashem for this witness. He lists the chain of festive days that follows from Shevat to Shavuos.

title.en: Israel lives on: Yaakov in Yosef's bones

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Dovid Melech Yisrael, Eliyahu and the eternity of Israel never died. He returns to the sea seeing Yosef's coffin: Yosef's bones carried the life of Yaakov, a sign that Klal Yisrael does not die, so the sea had to split. He applies this to each Jew who feels dead in his avodah: on Tu BiShvat he should take comfort that beneath the snow his roots are alive.

title.en: The Jewish ilan and fruit after its kind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the two Names joined together equal 'ilan', tree, from which all Jewish souls come, and no Jew can be cut off from it. The fruits of the Jewish tree must grow 'after their kind', looking like the fruits of earlier seasons; he warns of foreign cultures in America and of the claim that today's fruit may look different.

title.en: 'The G-d of my father': the sign of belonging

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shirah's 'G-d of my father' and the principle that the Torah does not change, and the Divrei Chaim that most leaders before Moshiach would be from the erev rav. The simple sign of who belongs to the tree is following the fathers' ways without new standards. He closes with Yosef's bones: those who carry Yaakov's warmth will cross the sea of the birth pangs of Moshiach and be planted in their land.

catalogTitle: ויסב אלקים את העם" - להיות מסובין על ה'.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Parshas Beshalach is one long lesson in emunah and bitachon, and that the forty years in which Hashem 'led the people around' (vayasev) were a forty-year haseivah, teaching every Jew, rich or poor, to lean on the Ribono shel Olam.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that Hashem led the people the long way so they would first learn Torah for forty years, and asks what that means for later generations. He calls the whole parsha a parsha of emunah: the Jews' trust in Moshe, their cry at the sea, the manna as a daily lesson that parnassah comes from Hashem, Amalek as doubt. The generation of the desert was the youth of Klal Yisrael and set its habit of learning. He then brings the Mishnah that even a poor man must recline at the Seder and the Midrash that derives it from 'vayasev'; with the Arizal's custom of leaning on the afikoman he explains that haseivah means leaning on Hashem through the matzah. Further sections treat swallowing a kashya with emunah, Serach bas Asher and the secret of the redemption, Miriam's song, Yosef as the 'ox', the haftarah, and the power of this Shabbos.

en: The whole of Parshas Beshalach, from beginning to end, is a parsha of emunah and bitachon.
The manna teaches that each day Hashem gives that day's parnassah, and that a person receives what is allotted to him, not more because he exerts himself more.
The generation of the desert was the youth of Klal Yisrael; like a young man's years of learning, it created the habit of Torah that later generations inherit.
Haseivah at the Seder is not about comfort but about leaning on the Ribono shel Olam, through the matzah, in which His Name is found.
The forty years of 'vayasev' were a forty-year haseivah, which is why the Midrash learns from it that even a poor man must recline.
A Jew must be able to swallow even a hard kashya and still hold on to emunah.
The redemption from Egypt was incomplete, a 'feminine' redemption, which explains Serach bas Asher's role, Miriam's separate song and Moshe's call to Yosef as 'ox'.

title.en: Why the long way through the desert

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Hashem led the Jews around so they would learn Torah for forty years before entering the land, and asks what advice that is for later generations. He then calls Beshalach a long parsha of emunah, the foundation of the whole Torah.

title.en: Emunah at the sea and in the manna

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the parsha: the Jews' trust in Moshe, their cry to Hashem out of the faith of their fathers, the Maharal's point that one acts on emunah even when not feeling it, the merit of emunah splitting the sea, and the manna as the lesson of daily parnassah.

title.en: Nothing left over for tomorrow

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who could not sleep while money remained in his house, and explains that the Torah asks a Jew to have today for today. He shows from the manna that effort does not change the amount, and describes how the tzaddikim learned and davened and found the manna at their door.

title.en: The jar of manna and the war with Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that bitachon is the fruit of emunah, brings Rashi that Yirmiyahu showed the jar of manna to a generation that would not learn, and says parnassah follows mazal, not effort. Amalek equals 'safek' (doubt), fought by Moshe's hands of emunah; with emunah everything becomes song.

title.en: The desert generation as the youth of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains shirah as order, then brings the Tanya that Klal Yisrael forms one complete body across the generations, with the desert generation as its head and youth. As a young man's years of learning create a lasting habit, the desert generation created the habit of Torah, which answers the opening question of the Midrash.

title.en: Even a poor man must recline

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that even a poor man may not eat on Pesach night until he reclines, and the Midrash that learns this from 'vayasev Elokim'. He presents the commentators' question on the connection, and Tosafos's reason for the rule: one might think a poor man's leaning, against a bare wall, is no haseivah.

title.en: Leaning on the afikoman, leaning on Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the afikoman is kept on the haseivah cushion, so one leans on the matzah. A mitzvah holds Hashem's Name, so leaning on the matzah is leaning on the Ribono shel Olam; haseivah is bitachon, which a poor man has as much as anyone.

title.en: A forty-year haseivah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the Midrash: in the desert, with the manna, Hashem made a forty-year haseivah, teaching the Jews to lean on Him. Since 'vayasev' is written there, it is a sign that even a poor man must recline, for in leaning on Hashem rich and poor are equal. He urges learning Beshalach in depth.

title.en: Swallowing a kashya with emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Tosafos's second reading (the poor man must wait until dark) and the difficulty from the Midrash, then the custom of eating kasha on Shabbos Shirah. He tells of the Chasam Sofer, who waited three days to answer his son's question, and says one must swallow even a black kashya, as after the tragedies of our time, and keep emunah.

title.en: Yosef's bones and Serach bas Asher

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah mentions Moshe taking Yosef's bones, and brings the Gemara that Moshe asked Serach bas Asher where they lay. Tosafos asks why her, and answers that the order of the redemption was handed to her, with the story from Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer of 'pakod pakadti'. The Mashgiach notes that this answer raises a bigger question.

title.en: Miriam's song and the halves of the matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the women sang a separate song after singing with the men, and why Moshe called Yosef 'shor' (ox). He brings the Chida on yachatz: the smaller half is the redemption from Egypt, the larger half is hidden for the final redemption, since the Jews left Egypt before the 400 years were complete.

title.en: Pakod yifkod and the ox of the Merkavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'pakod' equals 190, the years missing from the 400, and is a remembrance rather than a full redemption. He brings the Apter Rav on the brothers' plea to Yosef and the four creatures of the Merkavah, and the Megaleh Amukos that Yechezkel changed the 'ox' to a 'keruv', which Avraham and Moshe could not do.

title.en: The two haftaros: Devorah and Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Beshalach's haftarah is Devorah's song while Shvi'i shel Pesach reads Dovid's song. Through the Midrash that earlier songs are in the feminine and the final one in the masculine, he explains that Beshalach draws a temporary salvation, forty years of quiet, while Shvi'i shel Pesach draws the lasting salvation of Moshiach.

title.en: Serach bas Asher and Eliyahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Serach completed the seventy souls and the Yefeh To'ar's difficulty. He explains from seforim that one who brings good tidings is clothed with a spark of Eliyahu; Serach, who told Yaakov that Yosef lives, became fully Eliyahu, lives forever, and therefore knows the secret of the redemption, which was given to a woman because it was a 'feminine' redemption.

title.en: 'Come up, ox' and the women's song

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the threads together: Moshe called 'come up, ox' because the ox was not yet changed to a keruv and the redemption was not complete, so Yosef could not wait for techiyas hameisim. Hence also 'Hashem yimloch' in the future tense, and the women's separate song, a feminine song, which is the song Perek Shirah gives to the ox.

title.en: Drawing salvations on Shabbos Shirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says all the waters of the world split at the sea and the Torah is eternal, so through this parsha one can split every obstacle and draw salvations. He brings the passuk to remember the Exodus, the Ba'al Shem Tov on using every moment of Shabbos, and closes with Tu biShvat, when the Jewish tree begins to blossom, with blessings.

catalogTitle: פרשה מלא פנינים יקרים - מן זה אמונה' ימות המשיח' ושירת נשים.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that Parshas Beshalach is full of emunah, from the splitting of the sea and the mann to the shira of the women, and through the Rambam and Ramban on the days of Moshiach, ending with the call to leave this Shabbos with emunah and bitachon.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Chasam Sofer's question why the Egyptians drowned at the sea and not in the Nile: one may not return to Egypt, so only at the sea could Jews later make a brachah on the place of the miracle. He adds that the danger at the sea was a test of emunah, through which they merited the shira. He then shows that the whole parsha is full of emunah: the mann and its trace in the Shabbos cholent, Shabbos Shirah customs, and a story of the Stoliner Rebbe. Walking through the parsha, he finds emunas chachamim, techiyas hameisim, Moshiach and all thirteen ikkarim. The mann teaches that each person has his own channel of parnassa, which he ties to a Gemara on city names. He discusses the Rambam, Raavad, Radbaz and Ramban on whether nature changes in the days of Moshiach, and the Chasam Sofer on why the women sang only one passuk. He closes on the power of Moshiach's word, unity, and Tu Bishvat.

en: The Egyptians drowned at the sea rather than in the Nile so that Jews, who may never return to Egypt, could make a brachah at the place of the miracle.
The danger at the sea was a test of emunah and bitachon, and in that merit the Jews were granted the shira with ruach hakodesh.
The mann was food of emunah: each person received his own portion, so no one can take another's parnassa, and how much one works neither adds nor subtracts.
The whole parsha is full of emunah; all thirteen principles of faith, including techiyas hameisim and Moshiach, can be found in it.
Following the Ramban, nature was created to serve the tzaddik, and wild animals will return to their original peaceful nature when people stop sinning.
According to the Rambam Moshiach need not show wonders; his greatness is that by his word alone all Jews will follow him to Eretz Yisroel and unite in one Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Why the sea and not the Nile

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's answer why the Egyptians drowned at the sea: since one may not return to Egypt, only at the sea could Jews later make a brachah on the miracle. He adds that the danger at the sea was a test of emunah, in whose merit they sang the shira, and recalls Nachshon jumping into the sea.

title.en: The mann, the cholent and Jewish minhagim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the parsha is full of yeshuos, and that the Shabbos food, especially the cholent, carries a trace of the mann. He mentions the Shabbos Shirah custom, calls on a Jew to be able to swallow a question with simple emunah, and explains that minhagim come from the ruach hakodesh hidden in the whole of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The Stoliner Rebbe and the cholent

summary.en: After saying that stories of tzaddikim which are reliably handed down bring to emunah, the Mashgiach tells, in the name of R' Nosson Wachtfogel, how the Stoliner Rebbe in Williamsburg once spoke at length about cholent at the Shabbos kiddush and asked for a second plate, while that day there was no cholent at home.

title.en: Emunas chachamim and Moshiach in the parsha

summary.en: Walking briefly through the parsha, the Mashgiach shows emunas chachamim in the Jews turning back toward the Egyptians at Moshe's word, techiyas hameisim in 'Az yashir', Moshiach in 'Hashem yimloch', and individual hashgachah in the sea splitting into a path for each tribe and each Jew.

title.en: The mann as emunah; Amalek and Baal Tzefon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mann trained Jews in emunah: they left nothing for the next day, and gathering more or less made no difference, as with parnassa. He goes on to Amalek as doubt in emunah, Shabbos as testimony to creation, and Baal Tzefon, where the Jews davened only to Hashem, concluding that all thirteen ikkarim are in the parsha.

title.en: Each one his own channel of parnassa

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mann teaches that each person's food is prepared for him, so no one can touch another's. He brings the Gemara that expounds the city names Kinah, Dimonah and Adadah, asks why city names are expounded at all, and explains that each tribe, like each month and each mishmar, draws its parnassa from its own root.

title.en: The chassid, the mann at the door, and the borders

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Midrash about a chassid who learned from the hairs of the head that each one has its own source, and the Gemara that the mann fell at the doors of the tzaddikim. He returns to the city names: they hint that each one has his own border, so a person with bitachon stays silent when someone seems to take his parnassa.

title.en: Shiras hayam and the Rambam on Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls to 'eat' the parsha and to say the Shiras hayam with joy and together, noting that the shira ends with 'Hashem yimloch' and hints at Moshiach. He then brings the Rambam at the end of Hilchos Melachim that in the days of Moshiach the world follows its course and Yeshayahu's wolf and lamb are a parable, and the Raavad's objection from 'I will remove wild beasts from the land'.

title.en: The Radbaz, and nature as Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Radbaz that both are true: in Eretz Yisroel the pesukim will be literal, elsewhere a parable. He asks why the Rambam insists on this as a halachah, and explains that nature itself is the order of the Torah, bringing the Gemara in Shabbos that it was a disgrace that the order of creation was changed for a certain man.

title.en: The Midrash on Miriam's shira

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer on the Midrash that the angels complained why the women too should sing before them, and Miriam answered with the first passuk of the shira. He asks what the complaint was, what Miriam answered, and why the women sang only one passuk, and brings the Gemara in Megillah that women were also part of the miracle, with the Rashbam and Tosafos on the word 'also'.

title.en: Nature serves the tzaddik: the women's shira

summary.en: The Chasam Sofer answers that shira is said only on what is beyond nature, and nature was created to serve the tzaddik. The righteous women's rescue was therefore natural and only the downfall of the Egyptians was a miracle for them, so Miriam answered the angels with the one passuk about that downfall.

title.en: The Ramban, and the Raavad's objection explained

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban in Bechukosai that wild animals were created eating grass and became predators only through man's sin, and will return to their first nature in Eretz Yisroel when the mitzvos are kept. With this he explains the dispute: the Rambam cites Yeshayahu, where no condition of righteousness is stated, while the Raavad cites the passuk in Bechukosai, which is conditioned on keeping the Torah.

title.en: Moshiach without wonders

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Moshiach need not perform wonders, with the proof from Rabbi Akiva and Ben Koziba, and the Raavad who disagrees. He argues that the Rambam actually demands more of Moshiach: even Eliyahu's fire from heaven only moved the people briefly, while Moshiach will merely speak and all Jews will leave everything and go to Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The power of a tzaddik's word; one Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells what an old man in Tzfas remembered of R' Avraham Kalisker's words, like nails hammered into the heart, and explains that a tzaddik's speech is malchus. He contrasts the dispute that would break out today if someone built the Beis Hamikdash with the unity when Moshiach builds it and all groups of Jews serve together.

title.en: Full suitcases, and which tree to be

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that one should leave Parshas Beshalach with full suitcases of emunah, bitachon and simcha. Since this Shabbos precedes Tu Bishvat and Shevat is the month of eating, he says the fruits should be eaten like the mann, and brings Yirmiyahu's two trees, the man who trusts in people and the one who trusts in Hashem, calling on each person to decide which tree he wants to be.

catalogTitle: A Deeper Understanding of the עשר מכות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that each of the ten makkos revealed one of the ten utterances of creation, and that Barad, the seventh, was a rain of Malchus Shamayim which Moshe Rabbeinu asked to keep suspended for the Jews of the generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances, hidden inside nature, which the ten makkos brought into the open; according to the Zohar they correspond in reverse order, and each makkah struck Mitzrayim while healing the Jews. He explains the heavy heart of Pharaoh with the Midrash of the liver and the mashal of the heartless donkey, then shows other orders of the ten, including the Seder plate. Barad, the seventh, corresponds to Malchus and Shabbos. He asks why the Torah calls Egyptians 'those who feared the word of Hashem' only by Barad, and why Moshe went out of the city to raise his hands. His answer: Barad was a rain of Malchus Shamayim, cut short by Pharaoh's plea, and Moshe davened that it stay suspended to strengthen emunah before Moshiach. He ties Barad, which fell on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, to Shabbos and Torah.

en: The world was created with ten utterances hidden in nature, and each of the ten makkos brought one of them into the open, so that everyone could see who created the world.
Every makkah was an affliction for Mitzrayim and a healing for the Jews, which is why multiplying the makkos at the Seder draws healing down on Klal Yisrael.
Barad, the seventh makkah, corresponds to the seventh utterance, Malchus, which is Shabbos, the day a Jew accepts the kingdom of heaven.
Barad was a rain of Malchus Shamayim, bitter for Mitzrayim and sweet for the Jews; it gave even some Egyptians real fear of Hashem, but only while it lasted.
Moshe Rabbeinu's special tefillah with raised hands outside the city was that the interrupted Barad remain suspended, to help the Jews hold on to emunah in the war of doubts before Moshiach.
Barad fell on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, and Shevat, Shabbos, Torah and Barad are all one: genuine fear of Hashem comes only through Torah.
