title.en: Ten utterances revealed by ten makkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances, hidden inside every creature, and explains that the ten makkos brought them into the open, leading to the Ten Commandments. Following the Zohar he matches them in reverse order, and explains that each makkah struck Mitzrayim while healing the Jews.

title.en: Pharaoh's heavy heart and the heartless donkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kaved lev Paroh' with the Midrash that Pharaoh's heart was like liver, which hardens the more it is cooked, and tells the Midrash's mashal of the lion, the toll-collecting donkey and the fox. He repeats that the makkos were remedies for the Jews and urges learning these parshiyos in depth.

title.en: Other orders of the ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maggid Meisharim, where the makkos follow the utterances in straight order, and Rav Tzadok's explanation that holy things carry two characters, as with the different orders of the shevatim. He then shows how the Seder plate arranges the ten as three matzos and seven items, and how the seven makkos of Va'eira and the three of Bo match them.

title.en: Barad, Malchus and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Barad, the seventh makkah, corresponds to Malchus, which is Shabbos, when a Jew accepts the kingdom of heaven. He describes this fear of Hashem as awe that one enjoys, and brings that Bereishis spells 'yarei Shabbos'.

title.en: Those who feared Hashem's word, and Moshe's raised hands

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the pesukim of Barad and asks why only here the Torah calls Egyptians 'those who feared the word of Hashem', and how they could later chase the Jews to the Yam Suf with the horses that survived. He brings the Ramban on why Moshe went out of the city to spread his hands, and asks why this special tefillah was kept for Barad alone.

title.en: The suspended Barad and the war of Gog uMagog

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash Tanchuma that the Barad stopped by Moshe's tefillah stays suspended until it falls on the nations in the war of Gog uMagog. He explains that a spiritual war against emunah will come with it, that we are living in it now, and that seudah shlishis saves from it; he adds that a tzaddik's yeshuah comes easier for a non-Jew than for a Jew.

title.en: A rain of Malchus Shamayim cut short

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Barad rained down Malchus Shamayim, an acid rain for Mitzrayim and a sweet rain for the Jews, which is why only here some Egyptians are called 'those who feared the word of Hashem'. Pharaoh could not take it and pleaded, so only half the dose came down, and once it stopped those Egyptians lost their fear and used their horses to chase the Jews.

title.en: Moshe's tefillah for emunah before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his question: Moshe Rabbeinu did not go out to daven for Mitzrayim but that the Barad stay suspended, so that the Jews of the last generation, bombarded with thoughts of doubt, could draw yiras Shamayim from it, as at shalosh seudos. Such a high tefillah could not be said within the city and without spreading his hands.

title.en: Barad on Rosh Chodesh Shevat: Shabbos and Torah

summary.en: Following Rabbeinu Bechaye's dating, the Mashgiach shows that Barad fell on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, which this year falls on Shabbos, and links Shevat to Shabbos, to Moshe starting Sefer Devarim, to the Chiddushei HaRim's fresh crop of Torah, and to Shabbos as the day of Torah. Genuine fear of Hashem comes only through Torah; the Barad broke the trees of Mitzrayim while the Jewish tree began to blossom.

title.en: Va'eira: I appeared and I will appear

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes that the Torah is relived every Shabbos: 'Va'eira' means both 'I appeared' and 'I will appear', so the same Hashem who appeared in Mitzrayim with Barad appears to the last generation. He calls to use Shabbos Rosh Chodesh Shevat to take on learning Torah and blesses that it be the first Shabbos with Moshiach.

catalogTitle: שבת שירה - ביאור פנימי בענין שירה (שייכות לט"ו בשבט)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world was created with seven voices and is itself a song to Hashem, which Shabbos completes; on Shabbos Shirah and Tu b'Shvat every Jew is called to sing his part and to bear good fruit in Hashem's vineyard.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the meeting of Shabbos Shirah and Tu b'Shvat. Hashem created the world with ten utterances; seven of them became the seven days and seven middos, and Shabbos, the seventh, completes them and brings joy and song. Music needs exactly seven notes, so the world itself is a symphony and David HaMelech, the seventh, is song itself. He explains Kabbalas Shabbos, the Zohar's palace opened only by song, the seven seas with Kinneres as the harp, and Perek Shirah. Tiferes is harmony, the half-tones are the middah of din, and even the broken and silent parts of life belong to the song, as the blanks in Shiras HaYam show. A Jew who does Hashem's will conducts creation's song; a rasha sings only through his downfall. Hashem's own song is the vineyard of Yeshayahu, the Jewish people, and on Tu b'Shvat every Jew should begin to bear good fruit.

en: Seven of the ten utterances of creation became the seven days and seven middos, and Shabbos, the seventh, completes them and brings joy and song.
Because the world was created with seven voices, music has seven notes, and all of creation is a song to Hashem.
The palace of malchus and Shabbos opens only through song, which is why Lecha Dodi is sung to bring in Shabbos.
Even the sad, broken and blank parts of life are part of the song; one with emunah knows that everything is from Hashem and is good.
Every Jew who does Hashem's will is the conductor of the song of his part of the world, and when he does not act properly he spoils the whole symphony.
Hashem's own song is the song of His vineyard, the Jewish people, and on Tu b'Shvat every Jew, a tree He planted, should begin to bear good fruit.

candidateTopics: seven middos and the days of the week

title.en: Shabbos Shirah and Tu b'Shvat; the ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Shabbos Shirah coincides with Tu b'Shvat, and that two holy times strengthen each other. He introduces the ten utterances of creation: three are above this world, and seven became the days of the week, each matching a middah, up to Shabbos, the bride. He adds that before receiving the Torah a person must refine these seven middos.

title.en: Six days, seven shepherds, and Monday's division

summary.en: From 'ki sheshes yamim' the Mashgiach explains that the six days are six forces, and that the seven shepherds of Klal Yisrael, Avraham through David, match the seven middos. Monday, the day of din, is the first 'two', the root of division and machlokes, which is why 'ki tov' is missing there. Shabbos is the completion, and completeness brings joy and song, as at a wedding.

title.en: Kabbalas Shabbos; tiferes as harmony and healing

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how Kabbalas Shabbos follows the seven utterances: three times 'havu' for the three hidden ones, seven voices in Mizmor l'David, six chapters for the six days, then Mizmor Shir l'Yom HaShabbos. He explains tiferes as harmony, like colors in a painting or notes on a piano, and says healing comes from tiferes and hod, from balance, which is why a mi sheberach for the sick is made after the fifth aliyah.

title.en: Seven notes: a world built as music

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a niggun needs exactly seven notes, the eighth being the first again, because the world was created with the seven voices of 'Havu laShem'. The world is therefore a musical world in which everything sings to Hashem. The seven shepherds are seven keys, and only with the seventh, David HaMelech, can one sing; David is not only a singer but the 'sweetness of the songs of Israel' itself.

title.en: The palace that opens only with song

summary.en: David was the first Jew recorded playing music, for Shaul. The Mashgiach brings from the Zohar that there is a palace in heaven opened only by song, which David entered through song; it is the palace of malchus, of Shabbos. This is why Lecha Dodi, which R' Shlomo Alkabetz gave with two conditions, is sung before Mizmor Shir: it is the key that opens Shabbos.

title.en: Seven lands, seven seas, and the harp of Kinneres

summary.en: From Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer the Mashgiach brings that Eretz Yisrael is the seventh land, called 'zimras ha'aretz', and the Kinneres is the seventh sea, named for the harp. He cites R' Mordechai of Lechovitch, whose yahrzeit falls that night, that it is easier to believe the seven seas dried up than that a Jew who can sing does not sing on Shabbos, and explains it: every Jew is a small world with his own Kinneres, and Shabbos is the day of song.

title.en: Perek Shirah: all creation sings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Perek Shirah, where every creature sings to Hashem, and explains that the kosher animals sing as the chazzanim for the whole forest. Of the ten kosher animals in the Torah, three are brought as korbanos and seven are wild animals, and the seventh, the zemer, sings; man is the conductor. This is why Jews sing so many songs on Shabbos, culminating in Nishmas, where all creation merges into one great soul.

title.en: Seven strings, 'sova' as 'sheva', and harmony

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Arachin that the kinor in the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and in Moshiach's time it will have eight, learned from reading 'sova' as 'sheva'. He explains that such a reading is the verse's meaning: fullness comes only with seven, when the keyboard is complete. He then explains musical harmony, singing three notes apart, because the third middah is tiferes, and the chord with the fifth, which is hod.

title.en: Half-tones, minor keys and the middah of din

summary.en: The Mashgiach quotes the Yaaros Devash that angels and heavenly spheres sing in order, in tones and half-tones, rooted in kabbalah. A tune played only on the black keys, the half-tones, comes out sad, because halving is division, the middah of din. Each note and blend brings out a different mood; major keys come from chesed and minor from din, just as everything in creation comes from the blend of its voices.

title.en: Monday, the day of two, and Seder Moed

summary.en: Monday is the first 'two', the day of division and din; the Mashgiach mentions from the Arizal that one should not begin learning on Monday, and that people are careful about such things. In Chok l'Yisrael each weekday has its order of Mishnah, and Monday has Moed. He answers the question why Moed alone is singular: on the day of din one learns about the festivals to bring it joy, and keeps the name singular to strengthen its oneness.

title.en: Broken notes, tears, and the octave of teshuvah

summary.en: The tekiah is chesed and the broken shevarim and teruah are din, half-tones, yet they too are good: the Midrash reads 'bakosharos' as weeping and song together. The whole world is one niggun with major and minor parts that blend beautifully. Citing the Divrei Yisroel on R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev's saying, the Mashgiach explains that one who cannot reach the high notes sings an octave lower, the same tune, and this is teshuvah, the way of David HaMelech.

title.en: Emunah and the blanks in the shirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the world is one long symphony in which even the sad parts are beautiful, and a Jew with emunah knows that everything is from Hashem and good; only then can one sing. Shiras HaYam is written in the Sefer Torah like brickwork, with blank spaces, and the blanks are as much part of the song as the letters. So too the empty periods of a person's life, like rests in music, are part of the song.

title.en: Every Jew conducts the song of creation

summary.en: Every creature that does Hashem's will sings, as the tree with its growing and the bird with its flying. The Mashgiach explains Yehoshua's command to the sun: its shirah is functioning as Hashem set it, so to stop was to stop its song. A Jew is the conductor of creation: when he puts on tallis and tefillin and says Halleluyah, heaven and earth begin to sing; the neshamah is the finest instrument, and a Jew who acts improperly spoils the whole symphony.

title.en: The rasha's shirah and the song of din

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks when the rasha sings his shirah, and answers from 'vegam rasha l'yom ra'ah': on the day of his downfall. This explains why Esav's angel fought Yaakov just when his time came to sing: his song was his defeat, while David sings 'with my life'. From the Midrash he distinguishes the song of men, chesed, from the song of women, din, which is sweeter but belongs to the days of Moshiach; this is why Miriam sang only one verse.

title.en: No 'kashes' on Hashem; Hashem's own song

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the custom of kasha on Shabbos Shirah a hint, perhaps a joke, that there are no kashes on Hashem: all of Parshas Beshalach is emunah, and Rabbeinu Bachya says the sea split little by little. From the Chareidim he brings that singing to Hashem is a mitzvah, and since Hashem keeps all the mitzvos, he asks what Hashem's song is. He answers from Yeshayahu: the song of the vineyard, the Jewish people, whom Hashem planted in Eretz Yisrael and hoped would bear good grapes.

title.en: Every Jew a tree in Hashem's vineyard: Tu b'Shvat

summary.en: Hashem's song is all He does for Klal Yisrael, and He loves and sings over every Jew even when the grapes come out sour. From the Mishnah of 'kol Yisrael', 'netzer mata'ai', the Mashgiach says Hashem is proud of every Jew as a tree He planted Himself. Shabbos Shirah falls near Tu b'Shvat, the new year of the trees, and he calls on every Jew to begin bearing good fruit, in learning, davening and living as a Jew, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: מלחמה לה' בעמלק - קליפה של ליצנות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the power of Amalek is leitzanus, the joke that denies reality, and that the war against Amalek in every generation is the war against mockery of Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the war against Amalek in every generation and Chazal's image of Amalek jumping into the boiling bath and cooling it, and asks why Purim is celebrated with laughter and what the 'mockery' of Egypt in parshas Bo means. He shows the destructive power of leitzanus: one joke wipes out a hundred mussar talks, as in the story his rebbe told of a student who answered a drasha on the Livyasan with 'I don't like fish.' Analyzing laughter through the spleen, which Sefer Yetzirah assigns to Adar, he explains that a joke is the opposite of sechel and denies reality. Pharaoh survived the plagues by joking, so Hashem mocked Egypt measure for measure; Amalek, the jester, cooled the bath with a joke. Today Amalek jokes about the rebbe, the bachur and the Gemara, cutting the chain of mesorah, and Gog uMagog will fight Hashem with jokes. The Mashgiach calls on bnei Torah to reject leitzanus.

en: Leitzanus is the most destructive force: a single joke can neutralize a hundred mussar talks.
A joke is the opposite of sechel: what makes people laugh is its absurdity, its departure from reality.
Pharaoh and Egypt withstood the plagues by turning them into jokes, and Hashem therefore made a mockery of Egypt measure for measure.
Amalek's whole power is jokes, and that is why on Purim, in Adar, we turn laughter against avodah zarah and the wicked.
Amalek still remains and enters even the yeshiva, mocking the rebbe, the good bachur and the Gemara, and thereby weakening the mesorah from Sinai.
The final war of Gog uMagog against Hashem will be fought with jokes, and Hashem answers it with laughter.

candidateTopics: the nature of humor and laughter
Purim and the month of Adar
respect for the Gemara and the rebbe

title.en: Amalek who cooled the boiling bath

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the parsha's closing words on the war against Amalek in every generation and brings Chazal's mashal on 'asher korcha' of Amalek jumping into a boiling bath. He asks why Purim is celebrated with laughter and what the 'mockery' of Egypt in parshas Bo means.

title.en: The destructive power of leitzanus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a letz, unlike other sinners whom Gehinnom cleanses, does not merit to greet the Shechinah, because leitzanus destroys like nothing else. One joke wipes out a hundred mussar talks, as in the story his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel told of a student who answered a drasha about the Livyasan with 'I don't like fish.'

title.en: The spleen, Adar and what a joke is

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the spleen laughs and Sefer Yetzirah, which assigns the spleen to the month of Adar. He then analyzes a joke: it is the opposite of sechel, and the more absurd it is, the more it awakens the spleen, as onions stir the eyes and pepper the nose.

title.en: Laughter denies reality

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why simple people laugh at a sick or insane person instead of pitying him, and answers that what is opposite to sechel triggers laughter. He explains that a sense of humor helps a person endure troubles because it takes him out of reality into a world of fantasy; laughter denies the truth.

title.en: Pharaoh's jokes and Amalek the jester

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pharaoh withstood the plagues by making jokes about them, so Hashem's 'hisalalti' was mockery measure for measure. Amalek too was a jester: by jumping into the bath he made Israel's awesomeness a joke, and so on Purim, in Adar, the month of the spleen, we mock avodah zarah, the one leitzanus Chazal permit.

title.en: Amalek today: mocking the rebbe and the Gemara

summary.en: From 'vayachalosh Yehoshua' the Mashgiach shows that Amalek was only weakened and remains, entering even the yeshiva. A joke about the rebbe cuts the rope of mesorah reaching back to Moshe at Sinai; then come jokes about the good bachur and about the words of the Gemara, a poison that takes much mussar to remove.

title.en: Gog uMagog's war and the call to bnei Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tehillim 2 as the war of Gog uMagog, fought against Hashem with jokes because nothing else can push away emes, and Hashem answers with laughter. He ends by calling on bnei Torah to see themselves as Yehoshua's soldiers against Amalek: to reject leitzanus and be serious about Torah and mitzvos.

catalogTitle: מדארף זיך טובל זיין אין די פרשה!!

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach calls Parshas Beshalach a mikveh of emunah that a Jew must immerse himself in, and traces emunah through the splitting of the sea, the mann, the jar of mann, Amalek and the Shirah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling the parsha a mikveh of emunah in which one must immerse oneself. It begins with emunah: the Jews followed Moshe toward the sea without questioning, and the sea split only once they walked into the water. The mann taught them to trust Hashem day by day, the way people trust the sunrise only out of habit. From there he turns to thanking Hashem: Dovid HaMelech thanked Him for every breath, while we, lacking emunah, notice only large miracles. The jar of mann showed later generations that Hashem provides for those who learn Torah. Amalek is the power of doubt. A person with emunah sings, which is why this is the parsha of Shirah. After a story about dancing at Az Yashir, he lists the Sefer Charedim's six free segulos for atonement, calls Krias Yam Suf the root of all miracles, and closes with the mesiras nefesh of the Lubavitcher Rebbe whose yahrzeit falls that night.

en: The parsha is a mikveh of emunah, and a Jew must immerse himself in it, learn it through and live with it until it becomes part of him.
The mann trained the Jews to trust Hashem one day at a time, without worrying about tomorrow.
Dovid HaMelech thanked Hashem for every breath because he had emunah; people fail to thank because they notice only large miracles.
Amalek is the power of doubt, the same doubt that underlay Chava's sin and the question at Masa whether Hashem is among us.
Beshalach is the parsha of Shirah because one who has emunah sings and is not depressed even in exile.
Krias Yam Suf was the first miracle made specifically for the Jews, and all miracles in the world draw from it.

title.en: The parsha as a mikveh of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one must immerse oneself in the parsha as in a mikveh. He shows that it opens with emunah: the Jews followed Moshe toward the sea without asking, and the sea split only after they walked into the water.

title.en: The mann: trust for one day at a time

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Beshalach the parsha of the mann. People trust that the sun will rise only from habit, but the mann was a new miracle, and still millions of Jews believed Moshe and left nothing over for the next day.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for every breath

summary.en: Through the parable of a child and its caretaker, the Mashgiach shows how much one owes Hashem for daily needs. He explains that the last passuk of Tehillim sums up the sefer as thanks for every breath, describes the workings of the lungs, and says we fail to thank because we lack emunah.

title.en: The jar of mann, and Amalek as doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yirmiyahu showed the jar of mann to people worried about parnassah, and the Rambam at the end of Hilchos Shmitta v'Yovel on one who gives himself over to Torah. He then explains Amalek as doubt, linking the question at Masa to Chava's sin, and notes that Moshe's hands were emunah.

title.en: Emunah brings song; daily tests

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the parsha begins, runs through and ends with emunah, the foundation of all mitzvos, and that this is why it is the parsha of Shirah: a believer sings and is not depressed. Emunah is tested every day in small things, from rising in the morning to the fear of Heaven being like the fear of a person.

title.en: Shiras HaYam and a dance at Az Yashir

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls saying Shiras HaYam with fire and joy a diamond, and tells what he saw as a young man when Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz was in America: a grandson of the Chortkover Rebbe danced at Az Yashir, unashamed, and the Vizhnitzer Rebbe watched him with delight. He adds that one who says it with joy has his sins forgiven.

title.en: Sefer Charedim's six free segulos

summary.en: Comparing costly medicines to segulos that cost nothing, the Mashgiach brings the Sefer Charedim's six segulos for atoning for sins: answering Amen yehei shmei rabba with all one's strength, keeping Shabbos properly, saying Shiras HaYam with joy, hisbodedus with Hashem, and listening to a talmid chacham's words of yiras Shamayim.

title.en: Krias Yam Suf, root of all miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the plagues were aimed at the Egyptians, while Krias Yam Suf was the first salvation specifically for the Jews; the sefarim say all miracles draw from it. He describes the daily miracles of the body and calls Shabbos Shirah the time to take this to heart.

title.en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe's mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Noting that the Lubavitcher Rebbe's yahrzeit is that night, the Mashgiach describes his mesiras nefesh in Soviet Russia for yeshivos and underground chadarim, his arrest and release, and his answer to the interrogator who pointed a revolver at him. He ends with l'chaim.

catalogTitle: צפרדע - The Significance of the צפרדע's Song

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the frog, a creature of land and water and so a mixture of good and evil, sings 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso', the hidden unity that Hashem gives life even to tumah, which will become the greatest song when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the introduction to Perek Shira, where the frog tells David HaMelech that it sings more shira than he does, and with the Midrash on 'vata'al hatzfardea', where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argue whether one frog produced or summoned all the others. Using the Arizal's teaching that the ten makkos mirror the ten maamaros in reverse, he places the frog opposite yesod, and shows from the Midrash that it punished the Egyptians' attempt to mix kedushah with tumah. The frog, living on land and in water, is itself a mixture of good and evil. Such creatures cannot sing a passuk, so the frog sings 'Baruch shem', said quietly because it declares that Hashem sustains even tumah. The number two belongs to the sitra achra, which explains the machlokes. Citing the Imrei Emes, he says that in the future this song will be said aloud and become the greatest shira. He closes by applying yesod to the weeks of Shovavim.

en: Following the Arizal, the ten makkos repeat the ten maamaros of creation in reverse order, and the makkah of the frog corresponds to yesod, the attribute of kedushas habris.
The Mashgiach explains that a mixture of good and evil is worse than evil alone, because evil has no existence of its own and draws its life only from the kedushah held captive inside it.

The frog lives both on land and in the sea, so it is itself a mixture of good and evil, the measure-for-measure punishment for the Egyptians who wanted to mix Klal Yisrael's kedushah with their tumah.

'Baruch shem kevod malchuso' is said quietly because it declares that Hashem is present and gives life even where there is tumah, which, like the princess's craving in the Gemara's mashal, is true but not fitting to proclaim aloud.
Every creature in Perek Shira sings a passuk except the frog, which, being a mixture, sings 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso'.

In the future, when tumah will be removed and it will become clear that it never truly existed, 'Baruch shem' will be said aloud and the frog's song will be the greatest shira, greater than the Tehillim of David HaMelech.

title.en: The frog's boast to David and the one frog

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Perek Shira and its opening braisa, where the frog tells David HaMelech that it sings more shira than he does. He then brings the Midrash on 'vata'al hatzfardea': Rabbi Akiva says one frog produced all the others, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rejects this and says one frog whistled and the rest came.

title.en: Ten makkos as the ten maamaros reversed

summary.en: To understand the machlokes, the Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the ten makkos revealed the ten maamaros of creation in reverse order, matching them to the sefiros. The frog corresponds to yesod, and the Bnei Yissaschar reads the passuk in Tehillim that the frog 'destroyed' the Egyptians as making them barren.

title.en: A mixture of good and evil, and the amphibian frog

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the frogs came because the Egyptians wanted to kill the boys and keep the girls, to mix kedushah with tumah. He explains why such a mixture is worse than evil itself, then brings the Gemara that each creature on land has a counterpart in the sea, one tahor and one tamei, and notes that the frog lives in both.

title.en: Baruch shem said quietly, and the frog's song

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Pesachim that Yaakov Avinu said 'Baruch shem' and that it is said quietly, like a princess's craving for the scum of the pot, and explains with the Nefesh HaChaim that it declares Hashem's presence even in tumah. He then asks how tamei creatures sing in Perek Shira, and explains that the frog, a mixture, does not sing a passuk but 'Baruch shem'.

title.en: The number two and the machlokes resolved

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one is kedushah and two is the sitra achra, shown by the masechtos of tumah, Ohalos and Negaim, which open with the word 'shnayim'. Returning to the Midrash, he explains that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rejects Rabbi Akiva's single frog because the frog, a mixture, had to come from one and many together.

title.en: Baruch shem in the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Imrei Emes, who asks why Yaakov's 'Baruch shem' is not written in the Torah, and answers that when Moshiach comes it will become a passuk and be said aloud. He explains the difference between Shema, the upper yichud, and Baruch shem, the lower yichud that Hashem is present even in hester panim, and says that in the future tumah will be seen as never having existed.

title.en: The frog's song will become a passuk

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that in the future the frog's song, 'Baruch shem', will become a passuk like the songs of the other creatures and be the highest shira. He reads 'vata'al hatzfardea' as this future ascent, and explains that while the frog was hester panim for Mitzrayim, for the Yidden it was a revelation.

title.en: Fire and water, and the frog greater than Tehillim

summary.en: The Mashgiach quotes the Bnei Yissaschar that the frog's song is 'banu ba'esh uvamayim', says this is not in the printed Perek Shira, and suggests it comes from a teaching that the frogs that jumped into the fire said it. Returning to the opening braisa, he explains why the frog's song, now a croak, will be greater than David HaMelech's Tehillim.

title.en: Makkah and refuah, and the weeks of Shovavim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings 'nagof verafo', that each makkah was a blow to Mitzrayim and a healing for the Yidden, and asks what it meant that Moshe interrupted the frogs at Pharaoh's request; perhaps the Yidden were not yet ready for the full revelation. He closes by applying the frog's attribute of yesod to the weeks of Shovavim and the trials of today.

catalogTitle: פרשה של אמונה - נסיון דורנו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that Parshas Beshalach is a parsha of emunah, and explains that the trial of our generation, the last before Moshiach, is holding on to simple faith in a time of double hiddenness, like Avraham at the Akeidah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by showing that Beshalach is full of emunah: after the splitting of the sea the Jews reached the peak of faith, the mann is the foundation of emunah, and Amalek came when they asked whether Hashem is among them. He explains why he named his chevra Emunas Yisroel: tefillah itself is emunah. Avraham, the first believer, believed without the yud of chochmah, with simple faith. Purim, too, is emunah: Esther hints to hester panim. The Akeidah, Avraham's last trial, foretells the last trial before the geulah: to go on despite unanswered questions, as at Shema with closed eyes. Quoting the Ba'al Shem Tov, he describes a double hiddenness, which is history's month of Adar. He traces it to the world wars and to life among the nations, where the G-d-fearing are mocked, as the Gemara foretells. From Daniel and Malachi he concludes that believers must bind themselves together like roped mountain climbers.

en: Beshalach is a parsha of emunah: the sea, the mann and the war with Amalek all turn on faith.
Tefillah is an expression of emunah, since one who davens shows that he believes Hashem can help him.
Avraham's emunah, written without a yud, was simple faith without chochmah, like that of the grandmothers of old.
The trial of the Akeidah, to go on with joy despite an unanswered question, is the model for the last trial before the geulah.
Our time is a double hiddenness, history's month of Adar, when many do not even know that Hashem is watching.
Before Moshiach, believers must bind themselves together and strengthen one another, like mountain climbers roped together.

candidateTopics: Purim and the month of Adar
Ruzhiner parable of the mountain climbers

title.en: Beshalach, a parsha of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the parsha: after the sea the Jews reached the peak of emunah, the mann is the foundation of emunah, and Amalek came when they doubted whether Hashem is among them. He calls this a great Shabbos, since the whole essence of a Jew is emunah.

title.en: Why the chevra is called Emunas Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that when he founded the chevra he named it Emunas Yisroel so that its people would work on emunah, and explains that tefillah is itself emunah; even boys davening to win color war show that they believe Hashem can help.

title.en: Avraham's simple emunah without a yud

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Avraham's 'vehe'emin' lacks a yud, the letter of chochmah: his was simple faith without philosophy, like that of the grandmothers and of the Chasam Sofer's mother. He then notes that today there is great hiddenness and many questions on Hashem's ways.

title.en: Purim, hester panim and the Akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Purim the peak of emunah, touches on the Purim drinking, and links Esther to hester panim. He brings the Ramban that the Akeidah foretells the last trial before the geulah, and explains its trial as going with joy despite the question on Hashem's promise, as one accepts Hashem's kingship at Shema with closed eyes.

title.en: Double hiddenness and the month of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's two kinds of hiddenness with the parable of a child whose father is hidden in the house, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's fear of a double hiddenness before Moshiach. He contrasts Nisan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, the covered month, and says that in history we are now in Adar.

title.en: The hiddenness of our time

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes two aspects of today's hiddenness: the world wars, which uprooted the Jewry of Europe, brought new ideologies and the murder of six million; and life among the nations, which weakens Yiddishkeit until an ehrlicher Yid is mocked, as the Gemara at the end of Sotah foretells for the time before Moshiach.

title.en: Daniel, Malachi and the roped climbers

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Daniel's prophecy of an unprecedented time of trouble as the tzarah his generation lived through, and Malachi's 'az nidberu yirei Hashem' as the call for believers to gather and strengthen one another. He brings the Ruzhiner's parable of climbing a smooth wall and describes roped mountain climbers, concluding that Jews must work on emunah and stay bound together.

catalogTitle: אלקי אבי - להתקשר למסורת ישראל “עשה לך רב”

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that a Jew stays alive as a branch of the tree of Yaakov Avinu only by holding to the path of his fathers and attaching himself to a true rebbe and talmid chacham.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Kriyas Yam Suf and the Chazal that the sea fled when it saw Yosef's coffin, since Yosef had fled from sin. From the bit of life that remains in the bones, and from a tree that seems dead in winter yet blossoms in Nisan, he shows that the Jewish people never lose their life. Shevat means a branch: every Jew is a branch of the tree of Yaakov Avinu, and must ask in Shevat whether his home is still 'Elokei avi', the G-d of his father. He rejects the cry that times have changed, and says that in galus a Jew survives by cleaving to a talmid chacham who follows his own rebbe, coming to him with bittul as a vessel. Before Moshiach a great darkness will come, and only those bound to Yosef and the true shepherds will remain.

en: The sea split when it saw Yosef's coffin, because Yosef had fled from sin; the redemption is bound up with Yosef.
Like a tree that keeps its sap through the winter and blossoms in Nisan, the Jewish people keep a hidden life even when the nations despair of them.
Shevat means a branch: every Jew is a branch of the tree of Yaakov Avinu through the chain of his fathers, and must stay attached to it.
A Jew makes a home for Hashem only when what was kosher and treif for his father and grandfather is the same for him; this is 'Elokei avi'.
In galus a Jew's success depends on cleaving to a talmid chacham who conducts himself as his own rebbe did.
One must come to the rebbe as a vessel, with bittul and submission, ready to receive, not only to hear a nice vort.
Before Moshiach a great darkness will come; only the remnant who make themselves as nothing and are bound to Yosef will cross the future splitting of the sea.

candidateTopics: kriyas yam suf and Yosef's coffin
attachment to a rebbe and talmid chacham

title.en: The splitting of the sea and Yosef's coffin

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by speaking of Kriyas Yam Suf: the condition that the sea would split for the Jews, the Chazal that the sea split when it saw Yosef's coffin, and the names of the tribes that point to the redemption.

title.en: Yosef fled, so the sea fled

summary.en: After speaking of the stages of the redemption, the Mashgiach explains that the sea 'saw and fled' because it saw Yosef, of whom the Torah says he fled and went outside.

title.en: Yaakov Avinu and the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins a story some listeners have already heard and asks with what Yaakov Avinu merited more than Avraham and Yitzchak.

title.en: Yosef called 'bones' in his lifetime

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that because Yosef heard his brothers call his father 'your servant' and stayed silent, he was called 'bones' in his lifetime. He adds that a child carries in himself a part of his father, and speaks of Yaakov and his sons.

title.en: The life that remains: bones and a tree in winter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that after a person passes away a bit of life remains in him, from which he will rise again. So too a tree in winter looks dead, yet its life remains and it blossoms in Nisan; the nations despair of the Jewish people, but Jews identify with the tree and know its life is still there.

title.en: Shevat, the month of the tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew has a part in Eliyahu HaNavi and in Moshiach. Each of the twelve months belongs to one of the tribes, and Shevat is tied to the tzaddik, Yosef, and carries the tidings that life will return; now every tree must attach itself anew to its source of life.

title.en: The souls are the fruit of the tree

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jewish souls hang on the tree like its fruit, born of Hakadosh Baruch Hu and the Shechinah. A fruit that has fallen still looks like part of its tree and its owner does not despair of it; the avodah of Shevat is to ask whether one's halachos and minhagim still match those of one's fathers.

title.en: Times have changed? Not the Torah

summary.en: Citing 'I Hashem have not changed', the Mashgiach says Jews must keep the Torah, mitzvos and even light minhagim in the same form as always. He rejects the cry that times have changed, urges a bochur to remain a ben yeshiva after leaving yeshiva, and says one's home must be run exactly as father and grandfather ran theirs, since a small deviation keeps growing.

title.en: Elokei avi and the branches of Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether today's permissiveness is 'Elokei avi', brings the Kozhnitzer that the street has now come into the house and the Kotzker that Hashem is where one lets Him in, and says one makes a home for Hashem only by keeping one's fathers' kosher and treif. Shevat means a branch: the tribes are branches of Yaakov Avinu, and 'Shema Yisrael' is said to the Yaakov within each Jew.

title.en: Yosef's father's image and the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that what saved Yosef in his trial was the image of his father, and that Yosef carries Yaakov's line and the holiness of the bris. In galus Chazal's way to cleave to the Shechinah is to cleave to talmidei chachamim, and he brings the Yesod HaAvodah that the right talmid chacham is one who conducts himself as his rebbe did.

title.en: Following one's forebears and believing in the shepherd

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Reb Elchonon Wasserman at a seudah in Baranovich, who said that if he was wrong he could answer that great rabbanim told him so. A Jew must have a rebbe to guide him; from 'they believed in Hashem and in Moshe His servant' Chazal learn the duty to believe in the shepherds of Israel, and such a Jew remains recognizable as a Jew.

title.en: A Pesachdik vessel and the waters of Marah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a chassid of Reb Avraham of Slonim who asked for 'a dish for Pesach' and was told to send a Pesachdik vessel. One must come to the rebbe with bittul as a vessel; he brings the Chozeh of Lublin that at Marah the people could not drink because they themselves were bitter, and that a talmid chacham is called a tree, 'etz', because one takes counsel, 'etzah', from him.

title.en: A broken vessel; shepherds before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Karliner chassid whom the Ba'al HaTanya offered to make into a vessel, who answered that his rebbe had worked on him to be a broken vessel. One must go to the guide with brokenness, not as the modern man who knows better. He brings the Midrash on 'tell me, whom my soul loves' that in the darkness before Moshiach the young will be led to the shepherds.

title.en: Friends, the remnant, and the seed of redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses the worth of a chevra of friends, bringing the Stoliner's wish for one and a half chassidim in each town. There will be another splitting of the sea, for the remnant of His people: one who makes himself as nothing. From Egypt he shows that the first remembrance of redemption was a seed, even when the bondage then grew worse.

title.en: Who will come through the darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the great men of the time sense the redemption is near, but only those who live through the darkness will merit it, as in the plague of darkness in Egypt. Those bound to Yosef and to the tree will remain, and he asks that the chevros hold together and follow the true rebbes, not those who invent new halachos and minhagim for the times.

catalogTitle: מה שמועה שמע ובא? קריאת ים סוף ומלחמת עמלק

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach describes the signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha, the confusion and the test of emunah in the last generation, and learns from Yisro, who came to Moshe after hearing of Kriyas Yam Suf and the war of Amalek, that the only safeguard is to attach oneself to tzaddikim and to good, upright Jews.

abstract.en: Continuing a series on the coming of Moshiach, the Mashgiach explains why the calculated ketzin passed, and that there is a time fixed in creation when Moshiach must come. He speaks of Moshiach ben Yosef and ben David, of chevlei Moshiach and of war as a sign of redemption, bringing the Chasam Sofer that in a world war one should pray for Moshiach. From Daniel, Malachi and the Gemara in Sanhedrin he lists the signs of the last generation: great troubles, a Torah world that shrinks, the upright feeling small, and the erev rav growing strong. He answers a newspaper article that attacked the gedolei Torah, showing from the Gemara about Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai that Jews must follow the daas Torah of the tzaddikim even when a decree is sealed. He closes with Yisro, who saw that even after Kriyas Yam Suf Amalek could attack, and so came to Moshe: in such a time one stays a Jew only near the tzaddik and among good Jews.

en: The Mashgiach explains that besides the ketzin that depend on merit, there is a time fixed in creation when Moshiach must come even if the generation is not worthy.
A world war is a sign that redemption may be near, so the Chasam Sofer wrote that at such a time one should pray for Moshiach rather than only for peace.

Malachi foretells that in the last time the wicked will prosper and the upright will feel small, and then those who fear Hashem will gather and strengthen one another, and Hashem records it in a book of remembrance.

The Mashgiach holds that Jews must follow the daas Torah of the gedolim, whose counsel succeeds because they learn Torah day and night, and rejects the claim that they lack insight into public affairs.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's mistake came from Hashem because the decree of the churban was sealed, yet it was still far better that Jerusalem fell while Jews followed him.
The final test before Moshiach will be a generation of confusion, with chachamim on the side of holiness and on the side of the erev rav both bringing proofs from the Torah.
From Yisro the Mashgiach learns that after seeing that Amalek could attack even after Kriyas Yam Suf, one can stay a Jew only by coming to the tzaddik and living among upright Jews.

candidateTopics: Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David
Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai and the churban
Yisro and the war of Amalek

title.en: Why the calculated ketzin passed

summary.en: Continuing the talks on the coming of Moshiach, the Mashgiach asks why the ketzin calculated by Rishonim and Acharonim passed without redemption, and explains that there is a time fixed in creation when Moshiach must come. He compares it to Moshe's first appearance in Mitzrayim, after which the bondage grew harder before the redemption.

title.en: Moshiach ben Yosef, ben David and chevlei Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshiach is a comprehensive soul, joining the soul of Moshe with that of David, and that before it is complete it can appear in parts as Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David. He describes chevlei Moshiach and war as a sign of redemption, brings the Chasam Sofer on praying for Moshiach in a time of war, and the tzaddikim who said in the First World War that chevlei Moshiach had begun and the world would keep boiling like a pot before Shabbos.

title.en: Daniel, Malachi and the signs of the end

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Daniel about a time of trouble unlike any since Klal Yisrael became a nation, and Malachi's last chapter: the wicked prosper, the upright feel inferior, and then those who fear Hashem speak to one another and are written in a book of remembrance. He adds the Gemara in Sanhedrin that talmidei chachamim will diminish and new harsh decrees will come one after another.

title.en: Erev Shabbos of the world: a time of birur

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the time before Moshiach to a kitchen on erev Shabbos, full of cleaning and cooking: a time of birur in which old accounts are settled. He explains the great tragedies through the reincarnation of souls from the time of the churban, and uses the parable of a fly on a great painting, which sees only one black spot, to show that only the great tzaddikim see the whole picture.

title.en: The Gemara's signs: a generation that shrinks

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through more signs from the Gemara in Sanhedrin: the young shaming the old, the face of the generation, and a generation that keeps diminishing. He says that never in Jewish history has a generation shrunk steadily as it does now, when the world's population grows while assimilation and intermarriage reduce the number of Jews.

title.en: Talmidei chachamim and the erev rav

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the sign that talmidei chachamim will be despised, and that in this time the erev rav grows stronger; he brings the Divrei Chaim, who already wrote that many rabbanim of his time were of the erev rav. He returns to Malachi: when the upright are mocked and walk in shame, they gather in small circles and strengthen one another in emunah.

title.en: An article attacking the gedolei Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of an article in that week's Jewish Press by a rabbinic writer, who claims he does not attack the Torah, only the pretension of the gedolim to be its authorities. The Mashgiach says the writer had already written elsewhere that the Torah was written by different people, and that he blames the great rabbanim and Rebbes for Jews not having gone to Eretz Yisrael, where many could have been saved from the camps.

title.en: Daas Torah: the counsel of those who learn day and night

summary.en: The Mashgiach addresses the claim that Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai erred, and shows from the Gemara in Megillah that in every exile Hashem set up great Torah leaders, Chananya, Mishael and Azarya, Mordechai and others, who led the Jewish people also in public affairs. From the passuk that one who toils in Torah day and night succeeds in all he does, he explains that their counsel succeeds, and brings Rav Chaim's words on the authority of a Rishon who rules without a proof.

title.en: When the decree is sealed: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Yosef and Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Gemara itself says Hashem turned Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's wisdom back because the destruction was already decreed, yet Jews were right to follow him, and a churban that comes while following the tzaddik is far better. He compares it to the sale of Yosef, which brought Yaakov down to Mitzrayim with honor, and to Mordechai asking whether the decree was sealed in blood or in clay, and applies this to the decree of the recent destruction, which the tzaddikim saw could not be averted.

title.en: The fox and the fish, and the burned house

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Akiva's parable of the fox who invites the fish onto dry land: Torah is our water of life, and leaving it to escape danger is certain death. He tells a parable of a thief who set fire to the house he robbed and was then praised for saving people, and applies it to the Zionist leaders who claim to have rescued Jews; he adds Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words when the chief rabbinate was founded.

title.en: The final test: a generation of confusion

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rizhiner that the last test before Moshiach will be chachamim from both sides bringing proofs from the Torah, and that one must hold to those who keep the old Torah until Eliyahu comes. He answers the writer's mockery of following a Rebbe blindly, brings the Gemara that one who turns from evil will be considered mad, Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz that people will gather in small groups and whisper, and the Lechovitcher's blessing that his chassidim be healthy, fresh and 'meshuga'.

title.en: What did Yisro hear? Kriyas Yam Suf and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yisro had to come to Moshe in the desert after hearing of Kriyas Yam Suf and the war of Amalek, when he could have asked for instructions and learned Torah in Midian. He answers that Yisro saw that even after the greatest miracle Amalek could still attack, so in a world of scoffing one can stay a Jew only near the tzaddik and among upright Jews; he adds that it is better to believe what one need not believe than not to believe what one must.

title.en: Leitzanus, and holding on to the old faith

summary.en: In closing, the Mashgiach speaks of leitzanus, which can dismiss any truth by making it absurd, and of Dovid HaMelech, who was mocked yet did not turn from the Torah. He ends by urging faith in the chachamim and gedolim of the generation and holding on to the old way of emunah.

catalogTitle: The מכה of ברד and Its Eternal Benefits

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the makkah of barad, the seventh plague and the plague of malchus, brought down yiras Shamayim, that Pharaoh cut it short, and that its suspended remainder will fall before Moshiach and complete the world's fear of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that every Shabbos draws its holiness from its own sedra, and that the world was created with ten maamaros. Adam contains all ten, so he rules over creation, prepares his own food and progresses from generation to generation; in a digression he laments how modern inventions have taken away a person's rest. Bread, which shows man's distinction, is blessed with ten words. The ten makkos replayed the ten maamaros in reverse order, so barad, the seventh, corresponds to malchus, which is yiras Shamayim, Shabbos, and the month of Shevat in which it fell. The Mashgiach asks why only at barad some Egyptians are called 'fearing the word of Hashem', and how those same people could chase the Jews at the Yam Suf. He answers that barad brought down yiras Shamayim, but Pharaoh had it stopped; the hail still suspended in the air will fall before Moshiach. He closes with the Mishnah of Rosh Hashanah for trees and Beis Shammai's view.

en: Man is made of all ten maamaros, so he rules over the whole creation, and bread, his distinctive food, is blessed with ten words.
Each of the ten makkos manifested one of the ten maamaros, in reverse order, to show the world again that Hashem created it.
Every makkah that struck Mitzrayim brought a corresponding blessing to the Jews.
Barad, the seventh makkah, corresponds to malchus, which is yiras Shamayim and Shabbos, and it fell in the month of Shevat.
Pharaoh's plea to stop the barad interrupted the flow of yiras Shamayim, which is why the Egyptians who feared Hashem's word could later chase the Jews.
The hail that stopped in mid-air remains suspended and will fall before Moshiach, completing the world's yiras Shamayim.

candidateTopics: ten maamaros and the ten makkos
yerei dvar Hashem among the Egyptians
Rosh Hashanah for trees and Beis Shammai

title.en: Each Shabbos and its sedra

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that each Shabbos draws its kedushah from its own sedra, so one may not move even a passuk into the next sedra. He then begins a simple thought on the parsha: Hashem created the world with ten maamaros, which Kabbalah calls sefiros.

title.en: Man rules creation; the monkey only imitates

summary.en: Adam was made from all the maamaros, as the Ramban explains on 'na'aseh adam', so he controls everything. The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the builders of the tower became monkeys, the Gemara's image of a monkey imitating a man, and notes that only man prepares his own food.

title.en: Progress that enslaves

summary.en: Man alone progresses from generation to generation, but by using his wisdom for money and pleasure he enslaves himself. In a self-described tangent the Mashgiach contrasts the rest a person once had at home with today's telephones and cell phones.

title.en: Bread, ten words, and the sefiros

summary.en: Man was told to make bread, and the Shulchan Aruch notes that the brachah of hamotzi has ten words, corresponding to the ten maamaros. The Mashgiach explains the division into intellect (chochmah, binah, da'as) and the seven midos, and shows how each animal is built from one or two midos, the sheep from chesed and the lion from gevurah, while man contains all.

title.en: The makkos as the maamaros in reverse

summary.en: Seven makkos are in this week's sedra and three in the next, matching the seven midos and the three intellects. The Mashgiach explains that Mitzrayim was a rerun of creation: each makkah manifests a maamar, in reverse order, so makkas bechoros matches 'Bereishis' and choshech matches 'yehi or'. Each makkah also brought a corresponding blessing to the Jews.

title.en: Barad as malchus, and the first question

summary.en: Barad, the last makkah of the sedra, is the seventh, malchus, like the silver ke'arah under the seder plate. The Mashgiach reads the warning before the hail and Rashi's comment that dever struck only animals in the field, then asks why only at barad does the Torah say those who feared Hashem's word saved their animals.

title.en: The horses at the Yam Suf and the hail in mid-air

summary.en: Rashi says Pharaoh's horses at the Yam Suf came from the 'yerei dvar Hashem', so how could people the Torah honors with that title pursue the Jews? The Mashgiach tells how Pharaoh begged Moshe to stop the hail, how the hail froze in mid-air to fall at Gog uMagog, and the Ramban's question why only here Moshe left the city and spread his hands.

title.en: Malchus, Shabbos, Shevat: yiras Shamayim

summary.en: Barad is malchus, and malchus is yiras Shamayim, the kingship the whole world will acknowledge with Moshiach. Shabbos too is malchus, as the Yerushalmi shows that even an am ha'aretz is believed on Shabbos. Barad fell in Shevat, a month of yiras Shamayim, so the better Egyptians became 'fearing the word of Hashem'.

title.en: Pharaoh interrupts; Moshe's tefillah for the future

summary.en: Had the barad come down fully, the Jews would have left Mitzrayim and the world would have acknowledged Hashem, but Pharaoh had it stopped, so the Egyptians' yiras Shamayim ended and they chased the Jews. The rest of the hail will fall before Moshiach, as Yechezkel describes, and Moshe's special tefillah outside the city was for the Jews of the last generation.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah for trees and Beis Shammai

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes up the first Mishnah of Rosh Hashanah, whose unusual wording the Bnei Yissaschar asks about. He explains that maaser goes by the year of each tree's budding, and since in the days of Moshiach the halacha will follow Beis Shammai, a farmer who awaits Moshiach should note his trees now. He closes with the hope for Moshiach and the yiras Shamayim of the barad in Shevat.

catalogTitle: זמן קבלת התורה אפילו בלי הכנה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos Parshas Yisro is a second chance to receive the Torah even without preparation, because the Torah and its day stand above all calculation, and Hashem has special mercy on latecomers like Yisro.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the reading of the Ten Commandments in Parshas Yisro awakens the power of Matan Torah, so one who did not receive the Torah properly on Shavuos has another chance. Shavuos comes after forty-nine days of sefirah, but Yisro arrived without counting, and Shabbos, fixed by Hashem, needs no preparation. He then raises a question from the Masorah, which counts 72 pesukim in Yisro although one counts 75, and answers that the Ten Commandments are counted as ten parshiyos; the deeper reason is that whatever is connected to the Torah is above measure, like the Aron that took up no space and the fiftieth day that is not counted. The same applies to the parnassah of a talmid chacham, who is like Shabbos, and to the Rambam's words that anyone who devotes himself to Hashem throws off the yoke of calculations. He ends with Yisro, who heard of Amalek's attack on the latecomers and understood that it is never too late.

en: Reading the Ten Commandments in Parshas Yisro gives another chance to receive the Torah for one who did not receive it properly on Shavuos.
Shavuos comes after the preparation of sefirah, but Shabbos Parshas Yisro is for those who did not prepare, like Yisro himself.
Whatever is connected to the Torah stands above place, time and calculation, as the Aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim took up no space.
The parnassah of a talmid chacham, who is like Shabbos, is not bound by arithmetic, and the working people who support him are like the weekdays blessed by Shabbos.
Hashem's lasting anger at Amalek for attacking the stragglers shows His mercy on latecomers; from this Yisro understood that he too could still come.

title.en: A second chance to receive the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the reading of the Ten Commandments in Parshas Yisro awakens the power of Matan Torah, and that each Shabbos brings its own parsha. Shavuos comes after the forty-nine days of sefirah, but Yisro came without counting and without preparation, so this Shabbos is special for those who did not prepare.

title.en: Shabbos and the open heavens without preparation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Yomim Tovim, which depend on Beis Din's sanctifying the month, with Shabbos, fixed by Hashem from creation and needing no preparation. At Matan Torah the heavens opened before a whole nation; the haftarah of Shavuos tells of Yechezkel seeing the heavens open, while the haftarah of Yisro tells of Yeshayah seeing Hashem at once, without any preparation.

title.en: The Masorah's 72 pesukim in Yisro

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Masorah at the end of Parshas Yisro counts 72 pesukim, yet his own count gives 75. He explains that the Ten Commandments have two sets of trop and answers that the Masorah counts them as ten parshiyos rather than thirteen pesukim, a strained answer he accepts, citing the Chasam Sofer that most strained answers are true.

title.en: Above measure: the Aron and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives the deeper answer: there are wonders above nature and calculation. He brings the Gemara that the place of the Aron was not part of the measurement, because the Beis HaMikdash was a piece of heaven on earth, and explains that the fiftieth day of sefirah is not counted because it is a heavenly day. So too Parshas Yisro, the place of the Ten Commandments, is not subject to arithmetic.

title.en: The talmid chacham's parnassah and levels like Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Bnei Yissaschar showing people that their expenses exceeded their income, so their parnassah was above calculation, and applies this to talmidei chachamim. A talmid chacham is like Shabbos, and there are levels: like Shabbos, Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed or Rosh Chodesh. Those who work and support Torah are the weekdays providing for Shabbos, and each person must be honest about his level.

title.en: Shemittah, Shevet Levi and the Rambam

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shemittah is like Shabbos and brings the closing halachah of the Rambam's Hilchos Shemittah v'Yovel: Shevet Levi was set apart to serve Hashem and teach His laws, and he shows that most great poskim and roshei yeshivah were Kohanim or Leviim. Then he reads the Rambam that anyone whose spirit moves him may join and throws off the yoke of many calculations, linking it to the Masorah's sign for 72 pesukim.

title.en: Yisro, Amalek and the latecomers

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yisro was moved by the splitting of the sea and the war with Amalek rather than by Yetzias Mitzrayim. He explains that Amalek attacked the stragglers outside the Clouds of Glory, and Hashem is still angry at Amalek for this; Yisro, a latecomer after Matan Torah, saw Hashem's mercy on latecomers and came. He closes that it is never too late.

catalogTitle: "ועבדו לעולם" - "לעולמו של יובל" - לחזק באמונה עד ביאת עולמו של יובל (הגאולה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that an eved who did not finish his tikkun in the six weeks of Shovavim still has hope in Yovel, which stands above the world, and that before Moshiach the main task is to hold fast to simple emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by showing that each person's obligations in Torah are measured by his level: what would be nothing for a simple person counts as a sin for a tzaddik, as with Reuven, and what is beyond the letter of the law for others is the law for a great person, as with Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the porters. He then asks why Parshas Mishpatim begins with a connecting vav, and links it to the six weeks of Shovavim, with Mishpatim as the sixth and final week of the tikkun. After those weeks comes the power of Shabbos and simcha. For one who did not use the weeks, the eved who stays 'le'olam', the Mashgiach turns to Yovel: an eighth level above the seven-fold order of creation, rooted in the essence of the Jewish soul. He reconciles the Rashbam's plain reading with Chazal's 'until Yovel', speaks of the trials before Moshiach, and closes with the call for simple, wholehearted emunah, as in na'aseh venishma.

en: A person's obligations are measured by his level: what is a slight matter for a simple person is a sin for a tzaddik, and what is beyond the letter of the law for others is the law itself for a great person.
Parshas Mishpatim is the sixth and last of the weeks of Shovavim, the end of the tikkun, and so it is joined with a vav to what came before.
Yovel is an eighth level above the seven-fold order of the world, like the eighth day of milah, and it gives hope to one who did not complete his tikkun in its time.
The Jewish soul comes from beriah, creation from nothing, and therefore its root can never be damaged; from there comes the tikkun of the eved who missed the six years.
Before Moshiach the trials grow, and emunah becomes the hardest and most essential thing; one must believe simply, even without seeing.

title.en: Each person judged by his own level

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each person has his own level in Torah, so that Chazal's severe statements about tzaddikim measure them by their height. He brings Reuven and Bilhah as an act judged as a sin only because of Reuven's great level.

title.en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah and 'vachai bahem'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, whose porters broke his barrel of wine and who was told to pay them, and explains that what is beyond the letter of the law for others was the law for him. He then reads 'vachai bahem' by level: for a tzaddik, life itself means Torah, and for a great person even small details become a matter of din.

title.en: Mishpatim as the end of the Shovavim tikkun

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Mishpatim opens with a vav, as if continuing what came before, and answers with the six weeks of Shovavim, set aside by the early sefarim for tikkun. Mishpatim is the sixth week, corresponding to the sixth middah of Yosef, and with it the tikkun is complete; he also ties the weeks to the avodah that began in Parshas Shemos.

title.en: After the six weeks: Shabbos, freedom and joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that after the six weeks comes the power of Shabbos, of freedom and simcha. He tells of a man who asked a tzaddik how many fasts to do for his sins and was told that today the conditions are different, and says that Shabbos itself, enjoyed with higher pleasures of Torah and tefillah, is a tikkun, as the Eglei Tal writes.

title.en: The eved who stays: 'va'avado le'olam'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what becomes of one who did not use the six weeks, and finds it in the eved who did not go free after six years, of whom the Torah says 'va'avado le'olam'. Chazal read it as until Yovel, while the Rashbam explains it by the plain meaning as all his days; the Mashgiach asks how the Rashbam could say this against the halachah.

title.en: Yovel: the eighth, above creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yovel is above the creation of the world: the world was made in seven days, and the eighth stands before creation, which is why milah is on the eighth day. Yovel comes after seven times seven, beyond the order of nature, and so it brings a tikkun from the essence of the Jewish soul even to one who did not complete his tikkun in its time.

title.en: 'Le'olam' as the world of Yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Reb Chanoch, that Yovel is a release, and explains that when the Ribono shel Olam, who is above the world and nature, sends down that release, 'le'olam' means the world of Yovel. He distinguishes yetzirah, something from something, from beriah, something from nothing, and says the Jewish soul comes from beriah, which reveals that 'le'olam' is the world of Yovel.

title.en: Teshuvah from the root and the harp of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yerushalmi in which wisdom and prophecy are asked what the sinner's punishment is, and Hashem answers that he should do teshuvah, a tikkun from a root higher than all of them. He ties Shabbos Mishpatim to the world of Yovel and to Moshiach, brings that the harp of the Mikdash had seven strings and that of Moshiach will have eight, and says the forces of evil flare up most strongly just before they go out.

title.en: Holding on to emunah before the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the hard times before the geulah, a time of sorting out who will merit it, and the great reward of one who holds on to emunah then. He says that just as the avos nezikin come at the end of the Shovavim weeks, they are revealed more at the end of the sixth millennium, and that today one can achieve with Torah what earlier generations achieved with hard avodah.

title.en: Erev Shabbos of history: everything speeds up

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the present to erev Shabbos, when the kitchen is rushed and tense because Shabbos is near. He sees the same rush in the inventions that make work and communication ever faster, brings a tzaddik who said that before Moshiach Jews must move faster, and concludes that emunah is the hardest thing today and must be strengthened.

title.en: Simple emunah, na'aseh venishma

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for simple, wholehearted emunah in Hashem and His tzaddikim, as Klal Yisroel said na'aseh before nishma at Matan Torah, and brings Dovid Hamelech who felt like a beast before Hashem. He says that at the end of the exile, a people that can say na'aseh venishma will see the Shechinah return, and closes with the plural and singular in 'va'avadtem es Hashem'.

catalogTitle: “ואלה המשפטים” - דא רזא דגלגוליא (זוהר) - כח הסנהדרין לתקן עולמות ונשמות

oneLiner.en: Building on the Zohar that the laws of Mishpatim hold the secret of gilgul, the Mashgiach explains that the Torah's laws are the order of creation, so that the rulings of a Jewish beis din shape what is decided in Heaven and bring tikkun to souls and to the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar that 'these are the mishpatim' is the secret of gilgul, the way Hashem ensures that no Jewish soul is lost, and asks why the laws of the Sanhedrin are placed next to the mizbeach when the mizbeach lengthens life. Through the Maharal he explains that the Torah is the blueprint and order of the world, which is why Torah protects the traveler and the sick. He then shows how gilgul explains Hashem's hidden judgments: the Degel Machaneh Ephraim on losing a just case, the Ba'al Shem Tov's horse, the six million and the coming of Moshiach. Since the Torah's laws are the order of creation, a Jewish beis din's ruling is mirrored in Heaven, which is why Jewish cases must not go to gentile courts. He ends with Dovid HaMelech's rulings, Moshe Rabbeinu and the Maggid's students, and the haftarah of the freed slaves.

en: The Zohar teaches that the laws of Mishpatim, beginning with the eved ivri, contain the secret of gilgul: the order by which Hashem brings every soul to its tikkun so that no Jew is lost.
Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that the world exists for the Torah and the Torah is the order of the world, so attaching oneself to Torah attaches one to existence itself.
Humans see only a fragment of Hashem's judgments, like flies on one dark patch of a picture; seen with all past gilgulim, His judgments are true and just.
Because the Torah's laws are the order of creation, the way a Jewish beis din rules and the way Jews learn a halacha is how Heaven rules as well.

The Mashgiach explains that death by beis din, derived from 'from My mizbeach you shall take him', is not a shortening of life but a quick tikkun, since the mizbeach is the place from which the human body was formed.
Jewish cases must be brought before a Jewish beis din and not to gentile courts, since the redemption of Jewish souls depends on the rulings of Torah.

candidateTopics: Torah as the order of creation

title.en: The secret of gilgul and the Sanhedrin by the mizbeach

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar that Mishpatim holds the secret of gilgul and connects the eved ivri's six years of work and seventh-year release to the six weekdays and Shabbos. He then asks, with Rashi, why the laws of judgment sit beside the mizbeach, which is meant to lengthen life, and reads 'from My mizbeach you shall take him' as teaching that the beis din draws its power from the mizbeach.

title.en: Torah as the order and existence of the world

summary.en: From the Gemara on 'the sixth day' and the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that the world exists for the Torah, which is its blueprint and order, and that the ten utterances of creation unite many details into one. This is why the Gemara tells a traveler without company, and one who feels ill, to engage in Torah: Torah is existence itself.

title.en: Being cut off from Torah as part of a decree

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Hashem sometimes causes a person to neglect Torah so that he can be punished, and the Alexander Rebbe's explanation that Torah is a person's best friend, so being cut off from it is part of the decree. He adds the same about doubts in emunah, and the Kotzker's saying that dying by a Torah judgment is a great merit.

title.en: Gilgul explains Hashem's hidden judgments

summary.en: Returning to the Zohar, the Mashgiach says people see only a fragment of what happens, and brings the Degel Machaneh Ephraim: one who loses a case though he knows he is right may have owed the money in an earlier gilgul. He explains that each soul comes with a mission and returns until it is fulfilled, sometimes through gilgulim in animals, and lists the judgments a soul passes through.

title.en: Tzaddikim who die young, the six million, and the stoned ox

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that when a tzaddik dies young or six million Jews are killed, only Hashem knows the accounts of thousands of years; those killed al kiddush Hashem receive their tikkun at once, and tzaddikim connected to those souls heard from them that they see only chesed. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the punishment of an ox that killed a person is that its flesh may not be eaten, which delays its tikkun.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and the debtor's horse

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story, brought by the Chofetz Chaim, of the Ba'al Shem Tov who asked a wealthy host for a worthless debt document as a gift, tore it up, and the host's strong horse then died: it was the gilgul of the debtor, now freed. He connects this to the eved ivri, whose sale hints at a soul held in gilgul that a tzaddik can release.

title.en: A beis din below shapes the judgment above

summary.en: With the Maharal that the laws are the order of the world and the Chasam Sofer on 'before them and not before idolaters', the Mashgiach explains that each ruling of a Jewish beis din awakens the same ruling above. He applies this to the eved ivri's partial payment, shemitah and yovel, which embody Hashem's plan that no soul be lost and that Jews and all souls be redeemed.

title.en: Jewish courts and daas Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that learning Mishpatim or bringing cases to a Jewish beis din hastens the tikkun, while gentile courts rule for their own benefit, so Jewish cases must come before a Jewish beis din. The counsel of those with daas Torah succeeds even when it seems not to, and he rejects the complaint against the Polish tzaddikim who discouraged emigration to America and Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Mordechai, Yaakov and the birth pangs of Moshiach

summary.en: Speaking before Adar, the Mashgiach brings Mordechai, whose counsel not to attend Achashverosh's feast seemed to cause Haman's decree, and Yaakov, whose sending Yosef led to galus Mitzrayim: we do not see the whole picture. Before Moshiach Hashem settles all old accounts at once, and the six million souls were given a fast tikkun and will soon return as new souls to merit Moshiach.

title.en: Souls that will see Moshiach and the Chiddushei HaRim's kvitlach

summary.en: The Mashgiach reasons that just as the souls of the eigel returned to see the churban, the souls who endured the birth pangs of Moshiach will surely see Moshiach. He tells of the Chiddushei HaRim, who held two kvitlach, a woman in difficult labor and a dying man whose soul had to enter that child, and asks for whom to daven; he then discusses inducing labor and the mazal of a birth, concluding that we do not understand these matters.

title.en: Death by beis din as chesed, and the avodah of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his opening question: the mizbeach is where Adam's body was formed, so one executed by beis din receives a quick tikkun and can soon enter a Jewish body; what looks like din is the greatest chesed. He brings Rabbeinu Gershom's takanos and remembering Shabbos as examples of Heaven following what Jews do, and describes the avodah of Adar as revealing that Hashem runs the world even in hiddenness.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech's rulings and their reach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that Dovid HaMelech busied himself with questions of purity and checked his rulings with Mefiboshes, and asks why the king did not leave the ruling to Mefiboshes. He answers that Dovid's soul reached Atzilus and he was king of all Klal Yisroel, so his psak resounded in all worlds; a Torah act is not only self-improvement but changes the whole order of creation.

title.en: Moshe Rabbeinu, the Maggid's students, and the freed slaves

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke that the Jews agreed to other judges: had Moshe, the soul of redemption, ruled for all Israel, it would have brought the geulah, and he tells how the Maggid's students fell silent when asked who is the tzaddik of the generation. He closes with the haftarah, where the Jews freed and then re-enslaved their servants and so brought galus, and the Gemara that without Torah heaven and earth would not exist.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of the 4 לשונות הגאולה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the four expressions of redemption as the four exiles, shows how the ten makkos undo the ten utterances of creation in reverse, and finds in the makkah of barad, the 'Shabbos' of the makkos, a rain of yiras Shamayim that bears on the war against emunah before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the four expressions of redemption and the four cups, noting that each makkah struck Mitzrayim and healed the Jews, which he links to spilling wine at the Seder. The four expressions match the four exiles; just as the chazir, symbol of Edom, stands in its own passuk, the fourth expression stands alone, and Hallel over the fourth cup speaks of the final redemption. He then shows that yetzias Mitzrayim repeated creation: the ten makkos mirror the ten utterances in reverse, so makkas bechoros answers 'Bereishis' and choshech answers 'yehi or'. Matching the sefiros to the seder plate and to the days of the week, he places barad as the seventh, Shabbos. Barad rained yiras Shamayim, which explains the 'yarei dvar Hashem' and why they later pursued the Jews. The rest of the barad will fall at the war of Gog uMagog, a war against emunah; shalosh seudos protects from it. He closes with Rosh Chodesh Shvat.

en: Every makkah was at once a blow to Mitzrayim and a salvation for the Jews; the Mashgiach connects this to spilling wine from the cup at the Seder and then refilling it.
The four expressions of redemption correspond to the four exiles; the fourth stands in a passuk of its own because the redemption from Edom, the hardest exile, equals all the others.
At yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem showed the Jews a copy of creation: the ten makkos correspond to the ten utterances of creation, in reverse order.
Barad, the seventh makkah, corresponds to Shabbos, malchus and yiras Shamayim; it rained down yiras Shamayim so that even Egyptians became 'yarei dvar Hashem'.
The hail that Moshe Rabbeinu halted in mid-air will fall before Moshiach in the war of Gog uMagog, which the sefarim explain is a war against emunah.
Shalosh seudos, eaten in the dark, expresses emunah without seeing and protects from the war of Gog uMagog.

candidateTopics: ten utterances of creation and the ten makkos

title.en: Four cups, and makkos that were also healing

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the four expressions of redemption in this week's parsha and the four cups, and explains that every makkah struck Mitzrayim while bringing salvation to the Jews.
