From this he explains spilling wine from the cup at the Seder, the spilled wine standing for the makkah and the refilled cup for the salvation.

title.en: Four exiles and the fourth expression

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the four kingdoms, Bavel, Madai, Yavan and Edom, and describes Edom as the longest and hardest exile. Like the chazir, which stands in a passuk of its own, the fourth expression of redemption stands alone because the redemption from Edom equals all the others, and Hallel over the fourth cup speaks of that final redemption.

title.en: Ten utterances and the ten makkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'Bereishis' counts as the first of the ten utterances, and asks why the first of the Ten Commandments names Hashem as the One who took us out of Mitzrayim rather than as Creator. He answers that we did not see creation, but at yetzias Mitzrayim Hashem repeated it: the ten makkos mirror the ten utterances, in reverse. He frames the sefiros simply as the ten utterances and the seven middos.

title.en: Bechoros answers Bereishis, choshech answers light

summary.en: Going backwards, the Mashgiach matches makkas bechoros, the smiting of the 'reishis', to the utterance 'Bereishis', and explains that Mitzrayim worshipped the lamb, the mazal of Nisan, first of the months; at the same time 'my firstborn Yisrael' came to light. Choshech matches 'yehi or', while the Jews had light. Hashem undid each utterance for the Egyptians, while the Jews received its benefit in greater measure.

title.en: The seder plate, the seven days and barad as Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the ten sefiros on the seder plate, with the plate itself as malchus, and matches the seven middos to the seven days of creation, Shabbos being malchus. Using the seven 'kol Hashem' of Mizmor l'Dovid he places dam as chesed, water, and barad, the seventh makkah, as the Shabbos of the makkos, which struck the malchus of Mitzrayim.

title.en: The yarei dvar Hashem and the suspended hail

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah mentions those who feared the word of Hashem only by barad, and how these same Egyptians later chased the Jews with horses at the Yam Suf; what became of their fear of Heaven? He brings the Midrash that the hail Moshe Rabbeinu halted stayed suspended, part falling in Yehoshua's time and the rest before Moshiach, which the sefarim explain as the war against emunah.

title.en: Barad rained yiras Shamayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that barad, corresponding to Shabbos, rained down yiras Shamayim, citing Rabbeinu Bachya that it began on Rosh Chodesh Shvat, a name that echoes Shabbos. This answers his questions: the Egyptians were called 'yarei dvar Hashem' from the hail, not from within, and lost it when it stopped. Had Moshe Rabbeinu not been obliged to stop it at Pharaoh's request, it would have brought the world to Moshiach.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and the war against emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that keeping the three Shabbos meals saves from three judgments, and the sefarim who match shalosh seudos to the war of Gog uMagog, a war against emunah. Shalosh seudos eaten in the dark, like covering the eyes at Shema, is emunah without seeing. He describes today's war against emunah: missionaries, a world of apikorsus, and its entry into Jewish homes through the media.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh Shvat and this special Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the parsha's seven makkos end with barad, and that one should draw emunah and chizuk from learning the parsha with Rashi and Ramban. He notes that Rosh Chodesh Shvat is Rosh Hashanah for trees according to Beis Shammai, and that Moshe Rabbeinu began Sefer Devarim then. He closes that this Shabbos is a time to accept malchus Shamayim and receive the rain of emunah.

catalogTitle: הקב"ה מדקדק על האדם לפי מדריגתו; סוף זמן תיקון שובבי”ם

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem judges each person by his level, and that the six weeks of Shovavim, ending with Mishpatim, are the tikkun of the souls of Egypt, which is the key to the suffering of the last generations and to how a Jew holds on in exile.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by showing that the same act is judged differently by a person's level: the Zohar's severity about walking without washing the hands, the laws of yichus, Reuven and David, and the sensitivities of tzaddikim. Rabbah bar bar Chanah's porters show that for a great man the higher standard is the din itself, and the Mashgiach reads 'do not go up by steps on My altar' as a warning that for one who has risen, pride is like arayos. He then turns to the end of Shovavim: following the Arizal, the souls of Egypt were those of the generations of the flood, the dispersion and Sedom, and their tikkun is now done through toil in Torah. The Zohar on Mishpatim as the judgment of gilgulim, with a Ba'al Shem Tov story, explains suffering that seems unjust, including the churban of Europe and the complaints against the tzaddikim, as against Moshe and Mordechai. He ends with Esther in the beis hatzelamim, Yaakov's 'lagur', and the joy of Adar and Purim.

en: The Mashgiach teaches that the same act carries different weight according to a person's level; even halacha shows this, giving more laws to those who stand higher.
For a great person the higher standard is not beyond the letter of the law but the din itself, as Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chanah.
The six weeks of Shovavim, from galus Mitzrayim to 'naaseh v'nishma' at the end of Mishpatim, are a time of tikkun, and the main tikkun today is toil in Torah.
The Jews of Egypt were the souls of the generations of the flood, the dispersion and Sedom, who came back to be cleansed through the suffering of the exile.
'V'eileh hamishpatim' are, per the Zohar, the judgments of gilgulim: suffering that looks unjust is part of an accounting from earlier lives that no one sees whole.

The Mashgiach defends the tzaddikim of Europe against those who blamed them for the churban: like Moshe and Mordechai, they were blamed for the hardship at the end of an exile, while their concern was that Jews remain Jews.
Like Yaakov's sons before Pharaoh, a Jew who must live among the nations has to keep feeling that he does not belong there; the danger begins when he grows comfortable.

candidateTopics: tikkun of the souls of Egypt

title.en: Judged by one's level: washing the hands

summary.en: After a story of Rebbe Reb Bunim distancing a young man touched by Haskalah, who later mocked the Zohar that walking four amos without washing the hands carries a death penalty, the Mashgiach explains that the Zohar speaks to a higher level. Halacha itself, in the laws of yichus and of Kohanim, gives more laws the higher a person stands.

title.en: Reuven, David and Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tashlich

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chazal say Reuven and David did not sin, yet the pesukim speak of them as if they had, by the measure of their level. He tells how Rebbe Reb Elimelech said at tashlich that what is a mitzvah for a small man is an aveirah for a great one, and asks how anyone who knows what Moshiach is could think David sinned.

title.en: The fine senses of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells stories of tzaddikim who sensed a problem in food that was halachically permitted: a chicken with a shaila, and the Belzer Rav R' Aharon, who would not eat fruit that had lain on a dairy plate. What is permitted for ordinary people is, for great ones, a real issue.

title.en: The porters' barrel and 'do not go up by steps'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara of Rabbah bar bar Chanah's porters, where Rav ruled that he must pay them, and shows that for a man of his level this was the din, not beyond it. With the Gemara in Sotah that pride is like arayos, he explains 'do not go up by steps on My altar' as a warning to one who has risen, placed beside 'v'eileh hamishpatim' to show it is din.

title.en: Shovavim and the souls of Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the end of Shovavim, which the Arizal revealed as a time for teshuvah. In these weeks we read from galus Mitzrayim to 'naaseh v'nishma', and the Jews of Egypt were the souls of the generations of the flood, the dispersion and Sedom, who had to be cleansed before receiving the Torah.

title.en: Six weeks of tikkun and the toil of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the melachos of Egypt stand against the six weekdays, and the six weeks of Shovavim against them, with Mishpatim as the Shabbos, like the eved who serves six years and goes free. Bringing the Zohar's reading of 'avodah kashah, chomer, levenim' as kushya, kal vachomer and clarifying the halacha, he says today's tikkun is toil in Torah.

title.en: Adar, freedom and the kitrug

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that counting months from Tishrei, Adar is the sixth, the main time of tikkun, a month of freedom and of 'kiymu v'kiblu'. At such a time the Ba'al Davar raises a kitrug, and in Adar learning weakens in the yeshivos, which is exactly when one must strengthen it.

title.en: Naaseh v'nishma, Purim learning and pride

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties 'naaseh v'nishma' at the end of Mishpatim to 'kiymu v'kiblu' and tells the Kotzker's words on the father of the Avnei Nezer, who learned on Purim, adding that each time has its own avodah. He asks the bochurim to come to seder on time, and warns that one who has finished the tikkun of Shovavim must guard against pride, the 'steps on the altar'.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's lesson at the spring

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that 'v'eileh hamishpatim' are the judgments of gilgulim and tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov sent the Maggid to hide by a spring: a rich man forgot his wallet, a second man took it, and a poor man who came next was beaten by the rich man for it.

title.en: Judgments of gilgulim

summary.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov explains that the three were a litigant who had taken money wrongly, the man he wronged, and the careless dayan, now paying for his ruling. The Mashgiach concludes that a person who feels wronged by a din, or sees a tzaddik suffer, should know it is an accounting from earlier gilgulim; this answers Yirmiyahu's question and explains the suffering of Egypt.

title.en: Erev Shabbos of history

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the end of a tikkun to a kitchen on Erev Shabbos: hectic and rushed. We are in the sixth millennium, the Erev Shabbos before Moshiach; he brings the Zohar on the six hundredth year opening the gates of wisdom and explains the rush of modern inventions as the speed the final tikkunim require.

title.en: Blaming the tzaddikim, blaming Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that during the war people blamed the tzaddikim of Europe for not letting Jews go to America or Eretz Yisrael, an idea fed by the Yiddish press. He calls the apikorsim the guilty ones and shows it is nothing new: when the end of Egypt grew hardest, Dasan and Aviram blamed Moshe Rabbeinu.

title.en: The complaint against Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on 'Ish Yehudi… Ish Yemini': Klal Yisrael complained that David did not kill Shimi, from whom Mordechai came, and Shaul did not kill Agag, from whom Haman came. He shows that Mordechai was blamed for the decree although the Gemara gives another cause and Mordechai acted with mesirus nefesh, and that he went into exile with the Jews by choice.

title.en: That Jews remain Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the true tzaddikim lead by a mesorah whose first rule is that Jews remain Jews, and they knew that in America of that time they would not; he speaks of the assimilation he saw. The churban, he says, was the gathering of the tikkunim of all generations, like Yaakov's sending Yosef, which only seemed to cause the exile of Egypt.

title.en: Esther in the beis hatzelamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every generation has its Mordechai. Esther, forced into the house of Achashverosh, felt the Shechinah leave her in the beis hatzelamim and cried 'Keli Keli lamah azavtani'; today's exile is one great beis hatzelamim. One who is forced to be in such places must know the danger, daven as Esther did and prepare himself, as Mordechai did.

title.en: 'Lagur ba'aretz banu': Yaakov's formula

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Haggadah proves 'vayagar sham' from 'lagur ba'aretz banu', and answers that the proof is from the end of the passuk: before Pharaoh the brothers did not praise Egypt but said they came for their flocks. Yaakov taught his children to feel as strangers there, and so they did not assimilate.

title.en: Adar, Purim and erasing Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes with Adar as a month of joy and Torah. The Megillah is not history, Purim can achieve what Yom Kippur cannot, and he tells of a Purim seudah of the Stoliner Rebbe that was tied to Stalin's death. The greatest yeshuah is erasing the Haman in each heart; he ends with wishes for a good Chodesh Adar.

catalogTitle: בסוף שובבי”ם מתקנים אפ' “מה שבהמה פגמה”

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that by the end of Shovavim, at parshas Mishpatim, a person must be so repaired that even his animals and property do no damage, and that the higher a person stands, the more is demanded of him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the weeks of Shovavim, whose last Shabbos is Mishpatim, and with the Gemara's story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, which would not eat untithed food: a person's holiness spreads to all that belongs to him. He asks why the Gemara learns that 'mav'eh' means a person from a passuk about teshuvah, and explains that man was made upright, in the image of G-d, to build and repair; a person as such does not damage, only the beast in him does, so 'adam hamazik' is the man who repairs his damage. Through Kayin's complaint to Hashem, the guardian of the world, he teaches that one must appoint Hashem as one's guardian, as in Elokai netzor against lashon hara. He reads the Mishnah's first-person language as making a person responsible for his own middos, and shows from the Zohar, Chazal and the Rambam that what is demanded rises with a person's level, so that for bnei Torah at Mishpatim middos chassidus become din.

en: A person's holiness spreads to his possessions, as shown by Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, which would not eat untithed food.
Man was created upright and in the image of G-d, to create and repair; a person as such is not a damager, only the beast in him is.
'Adam hamazik' is the man who repairs what he damaged through payment, asking forgiveness and teshuvah; therefore the Gemara brings for him a passuk of teshuvah.
A person must appoint Hashem as his guardian, which is the meaning of asking in Elokai netzor that his tongue be guarded from lashon hara.
The more elevated a person is, the more is expected of him: what is a middah of chassidus for others becomes din for a tzaddik or a ben Torah.
At the end of Shovavim, at Mishpatim with all the laws of damages, a person must be so refined that his property too does no harm.

candidateTopics: man in the image of G-d as creator and repairer

title.en: Shovavim and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the weeks of Shovavim as a time to repair, and says that at Mishpatim, their last Shabbos, the repair must reach everything connected to a person. He tells the Gemara's story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, which would not eat untithed food, to show that a person's holiness spreads even to his donkey.

title.en: Why 'mav'eh' is learned from teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah of the four avos nezikin and asks why the Gemara proves that 'mav'eh' means a person from a passuk that Rashi explains as teshuvah. He begins the answer: Hashem made man upright and in His image, to create, sustain and perfect the world, and a man who does Hashem's will repairs everything around him, while a damager serves the four kelipos.

title.en: A person does not damage, the beast in him does

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has a G-dly soul and an animal soul, and only the animal in him damages; 'adam hamazik' therefore means the man who repairs his damage by paying, asking forgiveness as the Rambam requires, and doing teshuvah. This is why the Gemara brings a passuk of teshuvah for adam.

title.en: Kayin's complaint and the true Guardian

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on Kayin's answer 'hashomer achi anochi' as a complaint that Hashem is the guardian of the world, and says Kayin should have appointed Hashem as his guardian. He applies this to lashon hara, which the Gemara weighs against the three cardinal sins: the counsel is to ask Hashem in Elokai netzor, said several times a day, to guard one's tongue.

title.en: Hashem the Shomer and the spreading soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the deeper meaning of the Chofetz Chaim's prayer and of Elokai netzor: appointing Hashem as guardian. He reads the passuk 'amar shomer' behind 'mav'eh is adam' as speaking of the repentant man whose guardian is Hashem, and shows from Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's goats and from Rebbi and Rabbi Meir's staff that a person's soul spreads into his property.

title.en: 'Hichsharti': my ox, my responsibility

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the main guarding is that a person guard his own middos, anger, desires and habits. He notes that the Mishnah of damages speaks in the first person, unlike the Mishnah of Krias Shema, and reads this as a hint that when one's ox damages, the owner's own failings are responsible. At the end of Shovavim, at Mishpatim with all the laws of damages, a person must be refined enough that his possessions do no harm.

title.en: More is demanded according to one's level

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Zohar, brought by the poskim, calls one who walks without washing his hands in the morning chayav misah, and why Chazal and the Rambam compare arrogance and anger to the gravest sins. He answers that responsibility grows with one's level, as with a child, a bar mitzvah and a man of twenty, and illustrates it with a sack of potatoes versus a silk shirt with an ink spot.

title.en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the porters

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that Eretz Yisroel makes a tzaddik greater and a rasha worse. He then tells the Gemara of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, whose porters broke a barrel of wine, and Rav ruled that he must forgo the loss and even pay their wages; the Mashgiach explains that for a tzaddik, middas chassidus is din, and compares a king's dog to a minister who is punished for a small fault.

title.en: From the end of Yisro to Mishpatim: bnei Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the last passuk of Yisro, not to go up to the mizbeiach on steps, as a remez that a servant of Hashem must not be haughty, which is like giluy arayos. At Yisro that is derush, but at Mishpatim, after Shovavim, it becomes din; from bochurim who learn Torah much is demanded, to avoid anger and arrogance and make a kiddush Hashem. He closes with Shabbos Mevarchim Adar, the approach of Nissan and the geulah, and a brachah.

catalogTitle: עומק ישרות דיני תורה' להזהר במעשינו לפי מדריגותינו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the judgments of the Torah are just in a depth that spans gilgulim, and that the higher a Jew's level, the stricter the 'din' that applies to him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a story of the Ba'al Shem Tov: his talmidim watched an innocent man beaten over a lost wallet, and the Ba'al Shem Tov revealed that it settled a wrong ruling from an earlier gilgul. From this he asks how a beis din, where the Shechinah rests, can ever rule against the truth, and answers with the Zohar that 've'eleh hamishpatim' speaks of gilgulim: 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav', all generations taken together are just, as in the mashal of the gabbai who gives aliyos over many Shabbosim. He then asks why the Zohar and the Gemara say 'as if' or 'liable to death' for things the Shulchan Aruch treats lightly, and answers that souls stand at different levels, so more is demanded of a higher Jew. He illustrates this with kohanim, levels of tumah, shechitah, wine and a stained shirt, and with Rabbah bar bar Chanah, for whom acting beyond the letter of the law was the din. He applies it to Shabbos, to pride in avodah, and to the days of Adar.

en: When a Jewish beis din rules against the truth, the Mashgiach explains, it is settling an account from an earlier gilgul.
'Mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav': Hashem's judgments are seen to be just only when all generations are taken together.
Souls are of different levels, Asiyah, Yetzirah, Briah and Atzilus, and the higher the soul, the more is demanded of it.
The more refined and precious something is, the more sensitive it becomes, as seen in the kohen, in levels of tumah, in shechitah and in wine.
For a great person like Rabbah bar bar Chanah, acting beyond the letter of the law is itself the din.
A Jew who works on himself must keep Shabbos and his avodah on a higher plane, and guard against pride when he davens well.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and the lost wallet

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov had his talmidim watch silently as an innocent man was beaten over a lost wallet, and then revealed that this settled a wrong din Torah from an earlier gilgul.

title.en: How can a beis din rule falsely?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a beis din, where the Shechinah stands with the dayanim, can rule against a man who knows he is right, and answers from the Zohar on 've'eleh hamishpatim' that it repays an earlier gilgul: 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav'.

title.en: The mashal of the gabbai and the aliyos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a mashal of a guest who complains that the gabbai gives aliyos without order, until the gabbai explains that he reckons many Shabbosim together, and applies it to a person who sees only his own seventy or eighty years.

title.en: The puzzle of 'as if' in Chazal

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the many places where Chazal and the Zohar speak of 'as if' or 'liable to death', such as walking four amos without netilas yadayim, and asks why such things are not treated that way in practice.

title.en: Levels of souls, levels of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that souls come from Asiyah, Yetzirah, Briah and Atzilus, matching pshat, remez, drush and sod; the Shulchan Aruch is for every Jew, but from a refined Jew who works on himself more is demanded, and for him the Zohar's words apply.

title.en: The higher, the more sensitive

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the principle in halachah: a kohen and a kohen gadol in marriage, bread of chullin, terumah and kodesh in tumah, a potato, a bird and an animal in shechitah, and wine; then a mashal of an inked potato sack against a chassan's fine shirt with a tiny stain.

title.en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the porters

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Gemara of porters who broke Rabbah bar bar Chanah's barrel of wine, and Rav who told him to forgo and even pay them, saying this is the din; he explains that for a man of his stature, going beyond the letter of the law is the din.

title.en: A shirt, not a potato: Shabbos and avodah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the principle: a refined Jew is a shirt, not a potato, so his Shabbos must differ from that of one who waits for three stars to buy pizza, as 'beini u'vein bnei Yisrael' shows. He reads the end of Yisro, 'lo sa'aleh vema'alos al mizbechi', as a warning against pride in avodah, and links it to 've'eleh hamishpatim': for such a Jew, chassidus becomes din.

title.en: The days of Adar and Shabbos Mevorchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the world boiling like a lit firecracker before Moshiach, notes that Hashem prepares the cure before the blow as with Esther, brings the Gemara that a Jew's mazal is strong in Adar, and urges making Shabbos Mevorchim a whole Shabbos, closing with a brachah.

catalogTitle: The Basis of Jewish Faith

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the Rambam, that Jewish faith rests on the mass revelation at Har Sinai and its unbroken transmission, why this makes Hachodesh hazeh lachem the first mitzvah, and that this first mitzvah teaches renewal.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's question on the first passuk of the Torah: why not begin with Hachodesh hazeh lachem, the first mitzvah? But Mila and gid hanasheh came earlier. He recalls that belief in Hashem is instinctive to a Jew, yet since the Rambam counts belief as a mitzvah, it has halachos. He reads the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8: the Jews did not believe in Moshe because of his miracles, which could be magic, but because at Har Sinai millions of people were themselves prophets and heard Hashem command them to believe Moshe. A fact witnessed by a multitude and handed down cannot be refuted, which is why even Christians and Muslims accept it. Therefore every mitzvah, even Mila, is kept only because Moshe told us, and Hachodesh was the first mitzvah heard from him. As the first, it carries the quality of beginning: the new moon teaches a Jew always to renew himself.

en: Since the Rambam counts belief as a mitzvah, belief is not only an instinct; like every mitzvah it has halachos that must be learned.
Following the Rambam, the Jews believed in Moshe not because of his miracles but because at Har Sinai every one of them was a prophet and heard Hashem command them to believe him.
An event witnessed by a multitude and passed down through the generations cannot be invented or refuted, unlike claims that rest on individuals.
The Sefer Torah, written while hundreds of thousands of witnesses of Matan Torah were still alive, has stayed identical in every Jewish community.
Every mitzvah, even Mila and gid hanasheh, is kept only because Moshe told it to us, so Hachodesh hazeh lachem, the first mitzvah heard from Moshe, is the first mitzvah.
The first mitzvah, given at the birth of the nation, is a mitzvah of renewal: like the moon, a Jew who has darkened himself can always begin anew.

candidateTopics: Har Sinai as proof of the Torah

title.en: Rashi's question: the first mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah of Kiddush HaChodesh and Rashi's question why the Torah does not begin with it. He asks how it can be called the first mitzvah when Mila and gid hanasheh were given earlier, and finds the usual answer, that it was the first given to the whole nation, hard to accept.

title.en: Instinctive belief, and a mitzvah needs halachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that belief in Hashem is hereditary in the children of Avraham, can be spoiled like bodily health and restored, and that Hashem can be seen in nature and history. He then tells of a neighbor who sat in a sukkah with a plastic roof, to show that a mitzvah done without its halachos is not the mitzvah.

title.en: The Rambam: not belief through miracles

summary.en: Since the Rambam counts belief as a mitzvah, the Mashgiach turns to Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8 and translates it. The Jews did not believe in Moshe because of his miracles, which could be magic and which he did only for a need; a supernatural feat proves nothing. They believed because of what they themselves saw and heard at Har Sinai.

title.en: At Har Sinai every Jew was a prophet

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jewish faith, unlike Christianity and Islam, is not built on one charismatic person. At Har Sinai several million people each became a prophet, Hashem spoke to each face to face and commanded them to believe Moshe, and he brings the pesukim that show the covenant was with those alive and that the people would believe in Moshe forever.

title.en: A fact seen by millions cannot be refuted

summary.en: The Mashgiach argues that a public event cannot be invented: just as no one could deny George Washington or Julius Caesar, whom multitudes knew, the revelation seen by millions could not have been made up. He adds that the Sefer Torah was written forty years later while women, Levi'im and the young of Matan Torah were still alive to check it.

title.en: One Torah everywhere; the nations' claim

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that Jews scattered across the world for thousands of years have an identical Sefer Torah, differing only in one letter, and that the mitzvos differ only in small machlokesin. Therefore even Christians and Muslims accept Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah; he dismisses their claim that Hashem changed His mind, since Hashem knows the future, and says they watered the Torah down.

title.en: The third wall and the churches in Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells what he learned while in Yerushalayim: archaeologists found an ancient city wall beyond the present Old City walls, which would put the Christian burial site of their founder inside Yerushalayim, where the Gemara says no one but the house of David and Chuldah was buried. He relates that the Church then bought the land and built churches so no one would dig, and kept a plaque off the exposed stones; he calls this a tangent showing the falsity of their faith.

title.en: Halachah of emunah: believing a navi

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that in the Yad HaChazakah, unlike the Moreh Nevuchim, the Rambam gives the halachos of emunah: we believe because of the mesorah going back to Har Sinai, where Hashem appointed Moshe. He then asks why we should believe Avraham Avinu about Mila, since the Rambam rejects belief in individuals, and explains that even a navi like Eliyahu is obeyed only because Hashem commanded it, like the command to accept witnesses.

title.en: Even Mila comes through Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that we keep Mila and gid hanasheh and believe the stories of the Avos not because of Avraham or Yaakov or old records, but because Moshe, whom Hashem told us to believe, wrote them in the Torah. He adds that all religions fight over Yerushalayim because they cannot refute its holiness, and compares the absurdity of denying Sinai to a congressional resolution or to Holocaust denial.

title.en: The answer: the first mitzvah from Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Rashi: Hachodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah heard from Moshe, and once Hashem commanded belief in Moshe it became, retroactively, the first mitzvah. Mesorah alone is the uncontestable basis, though instinct and tzaddikim help. As the first, it has the quality of reishis, like the head that directs the body, so the Torah should have begun with it.

title.en: Kiddush HaChodesh: a mitzvah of beginning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah itself is about beginning: the new moon's rebirth, the first month, given to the nation at its birth at Yetzias Mitzrayim. Since Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim were created first, the month is declared only there by the high court, unless a greater chacham is outside the land, because the neshamah outweighs geography.

title.en: Renew yourself like the moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the lesson that the first mitzvah is renewal: one who has darkened himself should not let old memories say he cannot serve Hashem, but start anew like the moon. The nation was told to count its times by the moon, not the sun, and in Kiddush Levanah the moon is called a crown for those who will renew themselves like it.

title.en: Always new: Nisan and the new Mizbeach

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the secular New Year, stale by mid-January, with the Jewish count of every day as part of the new month, and says each morning a Jew should start again with new fervor and simcha. Nisan, when all of nature renews itself, is the head of the months; this power of renewal kept the Jews alive in Galus, and he closes with the new Mizbeach of the Rosh Chodesh Mussaf.

catalogTitle: בפרשה זו גנוז משה ר' ובחינתו אור הגנוז (שייכות לפורים)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's name is hidden in Parshas Tetzaveh not as a punishment but because his self-sacrifice bound him to the 'eighth', the hidden light above nature, which shines out again on Purim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with two levels of Mishkan: a Jew who is himself a sanctuary, and a sanctuary of wood and stone, matching Terumah and Tetzaveh as the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shovavim. He asks why the Midrash Tanchuma opens Tetzaveh with milah on the eighth day, and why Moshe's name is missing from the parsha. He explains that the world was made with seven lower utterances, while the 'eighth' is above nature: the hidden light, revealed on Pesach, Chanukah, Shabbos lights and at a bris, where Eliyahu comes because of mesiras nefesh, as a story with the Chasam Sofer shows. Yitzchak, born above nature, and Moshe, whose soul is from the hidden light, belong to the eighth. By saying 'erase me', Moshe bound himself to it, so his name is hidden in the eighth parsha. The talmid chacham who seems extinguished is stored the same way. Purim is a flash of that light in darkness; the Mashgiach ends urging bnei Torah to gather together on Purim.

en: There are two levels of sanctuary: a Jew who is himself the dwelling place of the Shechinah, and, after the sin, a sanctuary of wood and stone; Terumah speaks of the second and Tetzaveh of the first.
The world was created with the last seven utterances, so whatever is tied to nature is 'seven'; the 'eighth' is above nature and is the hidden light that Hashem stored away for the tzaddikim.
Milah is above nature, which is why it is on the eighth day and why Eliyahu, who comes through mesiras nefesh, attends every bris.
Moshe Rabbeinu's soul comes from the hidden light, so his life was a series of concealments, and by offering 'erase me' he bound himself to the world of the eighth.
The absence of Moshe's name from Tetzaveh is not a punishment but his greatness: his name is hidden in the eighth parsha, the parsha of the hidden light.
A talmid chacham who gives himself over to Torah seems extinguished in this world, but his light is stored away like the hidden light until the world is fit for it.
Purim is a flash of the hidden light sent down in a time of darkness, which is why Tetzaveh, the parsha of the hidden Moshe, is always read before it.

candidateTopics: seven and eight: nature and above nature

title.en: Two levels of Mishkan: Terumah and Tetzaveh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute whether the Mishkan was commanded before or after the sin of the calf, and explains that ideally each Jew is himself the sanctuary, while after the sin a sanctuary of wood and stone was needed. Terumah describes the building and Tetzaveh the kohen as the sanctuary, corresponding to the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shovavim; he also asks why the oil for the menorah is commanded here.

title.en: Milah in the Midrash and Moshe's missing name

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Midrash Tanchuma opens Tetzaveh with the law of milah on the eighth day and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's teaching that a father rejoices though he sheds his child's blood. He then brings the Baal HaTurim that Moshe's name is absent from Tetzaveh because he said 'erase me', and asks how that can be, and why the parsha hints at Chanukah.

title.en: Seven and eight: nature and the hidden light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the lower worlds were made with the last seven utterances, so 'seven' is nature and 'eight' is above it: the hidden light that will be revealed with Moshiach. He shows the eighth at the Exodus, in the eight days of Chanukah, in milah according to the Maharal, and in the Shabbos lights and the seven lamps of the menorah.

title.en: Candles, oil and the hidden light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of adding a Shabbos candle for each child through the hidden light, and says the kinor of Moshiach has eight strings. Oil, which rises above every liquid and can be lit, receives the light of the eighth; Chanukah, a time of the eighth, connects to the hidden light from which Moshe received the Torah.

title.en: Eliyahu at the bris and the Chasam Sofer's story

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Eliyahu, herald of the redemption, comes to every bris because milah breaks nature, and Pinchas earned this through mesiras nefesh. He tells of a mohel's mishap brought before the Chasam Sofer, where readiness to give up life brought a cure through Eliyahu, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that a mitzvah done beyond nature draws a salvation beyond nature.

title.en: Yitzchak and milah on the eighth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yitzchak, the first to be circumcised on the eighth day, was born entirely above nature. Using Rabbi Shimon's view that the Torah's reasons are expounded, he asks whether a child born on a day of 'eighth', like the first day of Pesach, must still wait eight days, and explains that the Midrash proves from Yitzchak, born on Pesach, that he must; this is why the Midrash fits Tetzaveh.

title.en: Moshe's soul from the hidden light

summary.en: Through Rabbeinu Bechaye and the Bnei Yissaschar the Mashgiach ties Tetzaveh to Chanukah and Moshiach, and explains that Moshe's soul comes from the hidden light. He shows concealment throughout: the hidden Chanukah oil under the kohen gadol's seal, the hidden miracle of Purim, and Moshe hidden as an infant, in Pharaoh's house and in Midyan, born as one who is milah itself.

title.en: 'Erase me': Moshe hidden in the eighth parsha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by saying 'erase me' Moshe overcame the instinct of self-preservation and bound himself to the world of the eighth, so his name was hidden in Tetzaveh, the eighth parsha of the book of redemption, with the eight garments of the kohen gadol and an ending that hints at Purim. The Baal HaTurim's reason is therefore not a punishment but Moshe's greatness.

title.en: The Lubliner's soup and the hidden talmid chacham

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Chozeh of Lublin spilled a plate of soup at his tish and Rabbi Mendel of Rimanov cried out in fear, until the Lubliner revealed it had foiled a decree against the Jews. From the gap between what is seen at the table and what happens above, he explains that a talmid chacham who gives himself to Torah looks extinguished, yet his light is stored like the hidden light.

title.en: Purim: a flash of light, and Purim Katan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tetzaveh is a preparation for Purim, when the hidden light flashes like lightning in the darkness of exile. He brings the dispute over feasting on Purim Katan and Rabbi Tzadok's explanation that in a leap year Purim of the first Adar is in the heart, and says Purim's hidden aspect can be felt even without its deeds.

title.en: Noach, Shes and Moshe; from Moshe to Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yalkut Reuveni's hint in the end of Terumah and the start of Tetzaveh that Moshe carried the souls of Shes and Noach, who survived while others were wiped out and did not pray for their generation. Moshe repaired this with 'erase me', rising from the outer level of seven to the inner level of the eighth, and his self-sacrifice returned in Mordechai, whose salvation came from the king's own palace as Moshe's came from Pharaoh's.

title.en: Gathering together on Purim

summary.en: Closing, the Mashgiach speaks of 'gather all the Jews' and the people of Mordechai, whom he identifies with the bnei Torah, and praises the plan for the yeshivah's young men to celebrate Purim and Shushan Purim together. He says eating and sitting together builds a love that learning together alone does not, and connects it to the unity of Shabbos.
